# ColivEase: full guides

> ColivEase is a Toronto rental platform built around roommates: a rule-based match score from area and commute, budget, move-in date, student or worker, gender preference and shared language; teams that apply together; optional ID verification badges and licensed-agent badges; every listing reviewed by a person; scam-line warnings in chat; neighbourhood scores with commute times, and whole homes you can rent room by room.

- Serves renters, roommates and landlords in Toronto and the Greater Toronto Area (GTA), Ontario, Canada, only.
- Roommate match score from area and commute, budget, move-in date, student or worker, gender preference (can be a must-have) and shared language. It follows fixed rules, not AI, and profile summaries are written from a fixed template. Roommates can form teams of 2 to 5 and apply for a home together.
- Language communities: roommates and homes rented room by room are shown to people who share at least one language with them; whole homes are open to everyone, with your own language community first. The app is available in 10 languages (English, Chinese, Korean, Spanish, French, Hindi/Punjabi, Vietnamese, Tagalog, Persian, Portuguese).
- Privacy first: profiles can use a comic avatar; each person decides, photo by photo and person by person, who sees a real photo and can take it back. A home's exact address stays hidden (maps show a ~350 m area) until the host accepts an application.
- Safety: every new listing is reviewed by a person before it goes live; scam lines in chat (such as "send the deposit first") trigger a warning; listings, people and messages can be reported or blocked; optional ID verification (Stripe ID, phone and email) gives a badge; licensed agents are checked against RECO and get a badge.
- ColivEase never handles rent or deposits: tenants and hosts arrange payment between themselves.
- Every listing shows neighbourhood scores (transit, amenities, safety, schools) and commute times, and whether the host lives in the home.
- Landlords can rent a whole home room by room (group renting): each room has its own photos and rent, renters apply for a specific room or as a team, and current roommates can be shown on the listing.
- Landlord mode is reviewed: hosts apply and are approved, usually within 48 hours, before they can post homes; owner-direct landlords can have 3 live listings for free.
- Prices in CAD, plus 13% HST: a free account (profile, match scores, homes, chat, scam warnings, 1 team); Gold membership $19.99/month and Diamond $29.99/month (more teams, an animated profile frame, a higher place in people search); optional ID verification $9.99 for 3 years; AI lease check $4.99 per lease (same price for members); pinned listing $49.99 for 30 days; tenant invite pack $29.99 for 10 invites; licensed-agent plans $199.99/month (5 listings) or $299.99/month (10 listings).
- Sign in with Google, Apple or an email link; you must be 18 or older. Without an account you can browse homes. Free on the web at https://www.colivease.ca/app.html; iOS and Android apps are on the way. Guides are in English and Chinese.

# Co-Living vs Renting Alone in Toronto: Which Is Better?

URL: https://www.colivease.ca/blog/co-living-vs-renting-alone-toronto/
Language: English
Updated: 2026-11-03

Co-living or a shared rental vs renting alone in Toronto: costs from CMHC data, privacy, flexibility, who is on the lease, who each suits and making it work.

For most people in Toronto, co-living or a shared rental is cheaper than renting alone. CMHC's October 2025 averages put a one-bedroom at $1,761 a month, while half of an average two-bedroom is about $1,023. Renting alone buys privacy, control and simpler legal arrangements. Sharing trades some of that for lower costs and company, and works best when you choose roommates carefully and know who is on the lease.

This guide compares the two on cost, lifestyle, privacy, flexibility and legal protection, and explains who each option suits.

## Key takeaways

- **Sharing usually saves money**, often several hundred dollars a month compared with a one-bedroom.
- **New leases cost more than averages.** CMHC found new tenants pay more than tenants who've stayed put.
- **Privacy and control** are the main reasons to rent alone.
- **Legal protection depends on the setup**, especially whether you share a kitchen or bathroom with the owner.
- **Shared living works when expectations match** and are written down.

## What counts as co-living?

People use "co-living" for a few different setups:

- **Co-tenants:** two or more people sign one lease for a whole unit.
- **Renting a room from a tenant:** one person holds the lease and rents rooms to others.
- **Room-by-room rentals:** a landlord or operator rents each bedroom separately, often furnished, with shared common areas. In Toronto, a home where four or more rooms are rented to separate people is a multi-tenant (rooming) house, and the City requires operators to be licensed.
- **Living with the owner:** you rent a room in the owner's home and share their kitchen or bathroom.

Each one comes with different rights, which we cover below.

## Cost: what the data says

### Average rents

U of T Student Life publishes averages from CMHC's October 2025 survey and the City of Toronto's 2026 average market rents:

| Unit type | CMHC average (Oct 2025) | City of Toronto average (2026) |
|---|---|---|
| Room | Not available | $1,146 |
| Bachelor/studio | $1,491 | $1,499 |
| One-bedroom | $1,761 | $1,763 |
| Two-bedroom | $2,045 | $2,055 |

Based on these averages:

- **Renting alone:** about $1,490 for a studio or $1,760 for a one-bedroom.
- **Splitting a two-bedroom:** about $1,020 to $1,030 each.
- **Renting a room:** around $1,150 on the City's figure.

### Why your quote may be higher

These averages include tenants who have lived in their units for years. CMHC's 2025 Rental Market Report found that, on average, new tenants were paying higher rents than sitting tenants. In Toronto, the average rent for a two-bedroom purpose-built unit that changed tenants was **$2,547** in October 2025, down from $2,612 in 2024. Even at that level, two people sharing would pay about $1,274 each, still less than the average one-bedroom.

CMHC also noted more competition from rented condo apartments in Toronto as owners shifted units into the rental market, which gives renters more choice in some areas.

### Other costs to compare

| Cost | Renting alone | Sharing |
|---|---|---|
| Utilities and internet | All yours | Split two or more ways |
| Furniture | Furnish the whole unit | Often only your bedroom; some co-living rooms come furnished |
| Rent deposit | Up to one month of the full rent | Usually your share |
| Household supplies | All yours | Shared |

See our guides to the [cost of renting a room in Toronto](/blog/cost-of-renting-a-room-in-toronto/) and [utilities for Toronto renters](/blog/utilities-for-renters-toronto/) for more detail. CMHC defines housing as affordable when it costs less than 30% of a household's before-tax income, a useful check whichever way you go.

## Lifestyle and privacy

**Renting alone**

- Quiet, your own schedule and your own rules
- Easier for working from home, night shifts, and hosting a partner
- No negotiating over chores, guests or the thermostat
- Can feel isolating, especially for newcomers

**Sharing**

- Built-in company and someone to split chores with
- Bigger or better-located homes become affordable
- Less privacy and more compromise: bathroom schedules, kitchen space, noise
- Your experience depends heavily on who you live with

## Flexibility

- **Renting alone:** you control the lease. To leave, you normally give your landlord 60 days' notice on Form N9, timed to the end of a rental period or the lease term.
- **Co-tenants:** leaving early is harder, because one person's notice can affect everyone on the lease. You'll usually need to agree on a replacement, with the landlord's consent.
- **Renting a room from a tenant, or from the owner:** notice depends on your agreement, which can make moving in and out faster, but also gives you less security.
- **Room-by-room rentals:** each room is often a separate agreement, so a roommate leaving doesn't change your rent.

## Legal differences: who's on the lease

| Setup | Who you deal with | RTA protection | Disputes go to |
|---|---|---|---|
| Renting alone | The landlord | Usually yes | Landlord and Tenant Board (LTB) |
| Co-tenants on one lease | The landlord, jointly | Usually yes | LTB for landlord issues; roommate money issues usually go to Small Claims Court |
| Room-by-room lease with a landlord who doesn't live there (including rooming houses) | The landlord | Usually yes | LTB |
| Renting from another tenant | The tenant | Often no | Your agreement; Small Claims Court for money |
| Sharing a kitchen or bathroom with the owner | The owner | Generally no | Your agreement; Small Claims Court for money |

Key points:

- The LTB's guide to the Act says a rental unit can be an apartment, a house, or **a room in a rooming or boarding house**, so renting a single room from a landlord who doesn't live there is usually covered.
- Most Ontario tenancies use the **standard lease**, which says, among other things, that terms banning guests or roommates are void and that assignment or subletting needs the landlord's consent.
- The **Residential Tenancies Act** generally doesn't apply if you share a kitchen or bathroom with the owner or their close family living there. Steps to Justice also notes it might not apply when you share housing with roommates. See [living with your landlord in Ontario](/blog/living-with-your-landlord-ontario/).
- **Co-tenants** are generally each responsible to the landlord for the full rent, so choose people you trust with money.

## Who each option suits

**Renting alone suits you if:**

- You work from home most days or work nights
- You value quiet and routine above savings
- Your income comfortably covers a full unit
- You're in a stable job and plan to stay a while

**Sharing or co-living suits you if:**

- You're a student, newcomer or early in your career
- You want a better location than you could afford alone
- You like company and don't mind compromise
- You want furnished, flexible options while you get settled

## How to make shared living work

1. **Choose roommates on habits, not just availability.** Talk about sleep, cleanliness, guests, money and noise before anyone signs.
2. **Know your setup** before you sign: co-tenant, roommate of a tenant, room-by-room lease, or living with the owner.
3. **Write a [roommate agreement](/blog/roommate-agreement-ontario/)** covering rent, bills, chores, guests, quiet hours and moving out.
4. **Split costs fairly.** Bigger rooms or private bathrooms can pay more; see [how to split rent fairly](/blog/split-rent-fairly/).
5. **Keep records** of every payment.
6. **Check in monthly** and fix small issues early.

## Find people before you find a place

## Bottom line

Renting alone costs more but gives you privacy, control and usually full protection under the Residential Tenancies Act. Sharing saves real money, often several hundred dollars a month, and can be a great way to settle into Toronto, as long as you pick compatible people, understand who's on the lease, and put your house rules in writing.

*This article is general information, not legal advice. For your specific situation, contact the Landlord and Tenant Board or a community legal clinic.*

## FAQ

**Is it cheaper to live with roommates in Toronto?**
Usually, yes. CMHC's October 2025 survey, as summarized by U of T Student Life, put the average Toronto rent at $1,761 for a one-bedroom and $2,045 for a two-bedroom, so splitting a two-bedroom costs about $1,023 each. Rents for new leases are usually higher than these averages, but the gap between sharing and living alone generally remains.

**What is co-living?**
Co-living usually means renting a private bedroom in a shared home, with the kitchen, living room and sometimes bathrooms shared. Some homes are run by an operator who rents each room separately, often furnished; others are simply roommates sharing a regular rental. The legal setup varies, so always check who you're signing with and what you're signing.

**Does the Residential Tenancies Act apply to shared housing?**
Sometimes. It generally doesn't apply if you share a kitchen or bathroom with the owner or the owner's close family who live there. Steps to Justice also notes it might not apply when you share with roommates, for example if you rent from another tenant. If you sign a lease directly with a landlord who doesn't live there, it usually does.

**Who should rent alone in Toronto?**
Renting alone suits people who need quiet and control, such as those working night shifts, working from home most days, or with strong routines, and whose budget can absorb a full unit's rent. CMHC treats housing as affordable when it costs under 30% of before-tax income, a useful check before committing.

**How do I make living with roommates work?**
Choose roommates with similar habits and budgets, agree on house rules before moving in, and write them down in a roommate agreement. Cover rent shares, bills, chores, guests, quiet hours and moving out. Keep payment records, hold a short house meeting each month, and raise small issues early.

## Sources

- [Rental costs in Toronto/GTA (U of T Student Life, using CMHC October 2025 and City of Toronto 2026 data)](https://www.studentlife.utoronto.ca/task/rental-costs-in-toronto-gta/)
- [2025 Rental Market Report (CMHC)](https://www.cmhc-schl.gc.ca/professionals/housing-markets-data-and-research/market-reports/rental-market-reports-major-centres)
- [National Housing Strategy glossary: affordability (CMHC)](https://www.cmhc-schl.gc.ca/nhs/guidepage-strategy/glossary)
- [Multi-tenant (rooming) houses (City of Toronto)](https://www.toronto.ca/community-people/housing-shelter/rental-housing-rights-information/multi-tenant-rooming-houses/)
- [Find out if the Residential Tenancies Act applies (Steps to Justice)](https://stepstojustice.ca/steps/housing-law/1-find-out-if-the-residential-tenancies-act-applies/)
- [Guide to Ontario's standard lease (Government of Ontario)](https://www.ontario.ca/page/guide-ontarios-standard-lease)
- [Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (Ontario e-Laws)](https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/06r17)
- [A Guide to the Residential Tenancies Act (Landlord and Tenant Board)](https://tribunalsontario.ca/documents/ltb/Brochures/A%20Guide%20to%20the%20Residential%20Tenancies%20Act.html)

# Dealing With a Bad Roommate in Toronto: What to Do

URL: https://www.colivease.ca/blog/dealing-with-a-bad-roommate/
Language: English
Updated: 2026-11-03

How to deal with a bad roommate in Toronto: raising noise, mess, unpaid rent and guests, mediation, your legal position by lease type, and when to call police.

Dealing with a bad roommate in Toronto usually comes down to three steps: raise the problem early and specifically, put what you agree in writing, and escalate only if that fails, through mediation, Small Claims Court for money, or the police for safety. Your legal options depend heavily on who is on the lease, so figure that out before you threaten anyone with eviction.

This guide covers the most common roommate problems, how to talk about them, and what the law in Ontario does and doesn't let you do.

## Key takeaways

- **Most problems are fixable with a direct, specific conversation** and a written follow-up.
- **Who is on the lease changes everything.** Co-tenants, roommates who rent from a tenant, and people living with the owner have very different rights.
- **Roommates can't evict co-tenants or change the locks on them.**
- **Money disputes between roommates** usually go to Small Claims Court, not the Landlord and Tenant Board (LTB).
- **Safety comes first.** Call 911 if anyone is in danger.

## Common roommate problems and how to raise them

| Problem | What to say or do first | If it keeps happening |
|---|---|---|
| Noise | Agree on quiet hours (for example, 11 p.m. to 7 a.m. on weeknights) | Write them into your roommate agreement |
| Cleanliness | Propose a rota with named tasks and days | Split the cost of a cleaner, or rebalance chores |
| Unpaid rent or bills | Send the exact amount and a due date in writing | Payment plan, mediation, then Small Claims Court |
| Guests | Agree on notice and overnight limits | Set a rule for when a regular guest pays a share |
| Safety (smoking indoors, unlocked doors, open flames) | Name the risk and the fix | Tell the landlord if it affects the unit; call for help if urgent |

### How to have the conversation

1. **Pick a calm moment.** Not at 1 a.m. in the middle of the noise.
2. **Be specific.** "Dishes have been in the sink since Tuesday" works better than "you're messy."
3. **Say what you need.** "Can we agree the sink is clear before bed?"
4. **Listen.** Your roommate may have a complaint too, or a reason you didn't know about (a new night shift, for example).
5. **Agree on one change and a check-in date.**
6. **Confirm it in writing.** A short message in the group chat creates a record: "As discussed, quiet hours start at 11 p.m. on weeknights."

If you share with several people, a short house meeting once a month can catch small issues before they turn into resentment.

## Put it in writing: the roommate agreement

A written roommate agreement won't bind your landlord, but it gives everyone the same rules and evidence if things go wrong. Cover rent shares, bills, chores, guests, quiet hours and what happens when someone moves out. Our [roommate agreement guide and template](/blog/roommate-agreement-ontario/) walks through each section, and our post on [guest and partner rules](/blog/roommate-guest-rules/) has wording you can copy for the most common flashpoint.

If you didn't write one when you moved in, it's not too late. Suggesting one after a conflict can feel awkward, so frame it as "let's make sure this doesn't happen again" rather than as a punishment.

## Unpaid rent and bills

Money is where roommate problems get serious fastest.

- **Keep records.** E-transfers with notes such as "Nov rent share" and screenshots of bills.
- **Send a clear written request:** what's owed, for what, and by when.
- **Offer a payment plan** if the person is genuinely struggling.
- **Protect the tenancy.** If you're co-tenants, the landlord can generally look to anyone on the lease for the full rent. Paying the shortfall yourself and recovering it from your roommate later may be better than risking arrears.
- **Last resort:** Ontario's Small Claims Court hears claims for money or the return of personal property worth up to $50,000. Your written agreement and payment records will be your main evidence.

## Your legal position depends on who is on the lease

### Co-tenants (you all signed the lease)

You each have a right to live in the unit, and none of you can evict the others. Only the landlord can end a tenancy, and in tenancies covered by the Residential Tenancies Act (RTA), that generally means using an LTB notice and, if the tenant doesn't leave, an LTB hearing. One of the LTB's landlord notices, the N5, covers interfering with others, damage and overcrowding, but an eviction can affect the whole tenancy, so it's rarely a neat way to remove one person.

What this means in practice: with co-tenants, negotiation is usually the only realistic path. Often the best outcome is agreeing that one person leaves and a replacement joins, with the landlord's consent.

### You're the tenant and your roommate rents from you

If you hold the lease and your roommate pays you, they're often treated as an occupant rather than a tenant of the landlord. Steps to Justice notes the RTA might not apply when you share housing with roommates, but the exact answer depends on your facts. That makes your written agreement especially important. If you want them to leave, give clear written notice in line with your agreement (or reasonable notice if it says nothing), and don't change locks or remove their belongings without legal advice. Steps to Justice's free "Do you share rental housing?" tool can help you work out which rules apply.

### You live with the owner

If you share a kitchen or bathroom with the owner, or with the owner's close family who live there, the RTA generally doesn't apply. The LTB can't help either side, and your rights come mainly from your agreement with the owner. See [living with your landlord in Ontario](/blog/living-with-your-landlord-ontario/) for how notice and deposits work in that situation.

## Mediation: a neutral third party

When direct conversations stall, a neutral person can help. Options range from a mutual friend everyone trusts to a community mediation service. Calling 211 connects you with community and social services in Ontario and is a good way to find mediation near you. Mediation works best when both people want to keep living together or want an orderly exit. It's not suitable where there's violence, threats or intimidation.

## When and how to leave

Sometimes the healthiest solution is for someone to move out.

- **Co-tenants:** the N9 is the tenant's notice to end the tenancy. One co-tenant serving an N9 can affect everyone on the lease, so talk to your roommates and the landlord before anyone signs one. A replacement roommate, sublet or assignment needs the landlord's consent. See [ending a tenancy with an N9](/blog/ending-a-tenancy-n9/) for timing.
- **Roommate of a tenant:** follow the notice terms in your roommate agreement and settle your deposit share before you go.
- **Living with the owner:** follow your agreement, or give reasonable notice if it's silent.

Whoever leaves, agree in writing on the move-out date, the final rent and bill shares, and how any deposit contributions are repaid.

## When to call the police or get legal help

**Call 911** if anyone is in immediate danger, there's violence or a threat of violence, someone is breaking in, or there's a fire or medical emergency.

**Call the Toronto Police non-emergency line** for non-urgent crimes, such as a roommate taking your belongings or ongoing harassment.

**Call 211 for a mental health crisis.** The City's Toronto Community Crisis Service sends trained crisis workers, without police, to people 16 and older, 24 hours a day.

**Get legal help** if someone is threatening to lock you out, you're being asked to leave and aren't sure of your rights, or a lot of money is involved. Community legal clinics funded by Legal Aid Ontario give free or low-cost advice; call 1-800-668-8258 or use LAO's online directory. For questions about LTB processes, the LTB's line is 1-888-332-3234.

## Avoid the next bad roommate

## Bottom line

Raise problems early, be specific, and write down what you agree. Know which category you're in, because co-tenants can't evict each other, roommates of a tenant depend on their agreement, and people living with the owner usually fall outside the RTA. Use Small Claims Court for money, the police for safety, and a legal clinic before you take any step you can't undo.

*This article is general information, not legal advice. For your specific situation, contact the Landlord and Tenant Board or a community legal clinic.*

## FAQ

**Can I evict my roommate in Ontario?**
It depends on who is on the lease. If you're co-tenants, you can't evict each other; only the landlord can end a tenancy, normally through the Landlord and Tenant Board. If your roommate pays you and isn't on the lease, the RTA often doesn't apply between you, so your written agreement and reasonable notice matter most. Get legal advice before acting.

**Can I change the locks to keep my roommate out?**
Don't. If your roommate is a co-tenant, they have the same right to live in the unit as you do, and locking them out can create legal trouble for you. Even when the Residential Tenancies Act doesn't apply, removing someone or their belongings without proper notice is risky. Talk to a community legal clinic first.

**What can I do if my roommate won't pay their share of the rent?**
Put the amount owed in writing, keep payment records, and agree on a deadline. If you're co-tenants, the landlord can usually expect the full rent from anyone on the lease, so cover the shortfall if you can to protect the tenancy. You can then try mediation or sue your roommate in Small Claims Court, which hears claims up to $50,000.

**Does the Landlord and Tenant Board handle roommate disputes?**
Generally no. The LTB decides disputes between landlords and tenants under the Residential Tenancies Act. Arguments between roommates about chores, guests or unpaid shares usually aren't LTB matters. Money disputes between roommates normally go to Small Claims Court, and safety issues go to the police.

**When should I call the police about a roommate?**
Call 911 if anyone is in immediate danger, there's violence or a threat of violence, or someone is breaking in. Use the Toronto Police non-emergency line for things like theft of your belongings or ongoing harassment. For a mental health crisis, you can call 211 to reach the Toronto Community Crisis Service.

## Sources

- [Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (Ontario e-Laws)](https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/06r17)
- [Find out if the Residential Tenancies Act applies (Steps to Justice)](https://stepstojustice.ca/steps/housing-law/1-find-out-if-the-residential-tenancies-act-applies/)
- [Do you share rental housing? Interactive tool (Steps to Justice)](https://stepstojustice.ca/resource/do-you-share-rental-housing/)
- [Small Claims Court (Superior Court of Justice)](https://www.ontariocourts.ca/scj/areas-of-law/small-claims-court/)
- [Forms: N5 and N9 notices (Landlord and Tenant Board)](https://tribunalsontario.ca/ltb/forms-filing-and-fees/)
- [Renting in Ontario: Your rights (Government of Ontario)](https://www.ontario.ca/page/renting-ontario-your-rights)
- [Find a legal clinic (Legal Aid Ontario)](https://www.legalaid.on.ca/legal-clinics/)
- [Toronto Community Crisis Service (City of Toronto)](https://www.toronto.ca/community-people/public-safety-alerts/community-safety-wellbeing-programs/toronto-community-crisis-service/)

# Landlord Entry Rules Ontario: 24-Hour Notice Explained

URL: https://www.colivease.ca/blog/landlord-entry-rules-ontario/
Language: English
Updated: 2026-11-03

Landlord entry rules in Ontario: when 24 hours' written notice is needed, the 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. window, emergencies, showings and what to do if rules are broken.

In Ontario, your landlord usually needs to give you **at least 24 hours' written notice** before entering your unit, stating the reason, the date and a time between **8 a.m. and 8 p.m.** The main exceptions are emergencies, entry you agree to at the time, cleaning your lease includes, and showings to new tenants after a notice to end your tenancy. If your landlord ignores these rules, you can file a Form T2 with the Landlord and Tenant Board (LTB).

Your home is still your home when you rent it. Here's exactly when a landlord can come in, what a proper notice looks like, and what to do when the line gets crossed.

## Key takeaways

- **Standard rule:** written notice at least 24 hours ahead, with reason, date and a time between 8 a.m. and 8 p.m.
- **Only certain reasons count,** such as repairs, inspections, and viewings by a buyer, lender or insurer.
- **No notice needed** for emergencies, entry you consent to at the time, agreed cleaning, or showings after a notice to end the tenancy (8 a.m. to 8 p.m., after the landlord tries to tell you).
- **Repairs you asked for still need notice** unless you agree on the spot.
- **You can't block a valid entry,** but you can stay home while it happens.
- **Broken rules?** Document it, then file a T2 within one year. Illegal entry is also an offence under the Residential Tenancies Act (RTA).

*This article is general information, not legal advice. For your situation, contact the [Landlord and Tenant Board](https://tribunalsontario.ca/ltb/) or a community legal clinic (Legal Aid Ontario can refer you to one at 1-800-668-8258).*

## First: do these rules apply to you?

The entry rules come from sections 26 and 27 of the RTA, which covers most rentals in Ontario: apartments, condos, houses, basement units and rooming houses. If you **share a kitchen or bathroom with the owner** who lives there, the RTA generally doesn't apply, and the owner doesn't need to give notice to use shared space. Get clear house rules in writing before you move in. Our guide to [living with your landlord](/blog/living-with-your-landlord-ontario/) covers that setup.

## Entry with 24 hours' written notice

A landlord can enter with proper written notice for these reasons only:

1. To make a repair or replacement, or do work in the unit
2. To let a potential mortgage lender or insurer view the unit
3. To let an engineer, architect or other qualified person inspect the unit when the Condominium Act requires it
4. To inspect whether the unit is in good repair and meets health, safety, housing and maintenance standards, if the inspection is reasonable
5. For another reasonable reason written into your lease
6. To show the unit to a **potential buyer** (a registered real estate agent can do this with the landlord's written authorization)
7. To check that an air conditioner you installed is safe, secure and not causing damage

"I just want to see how you're keeping the place" isn't on the list. Neither is dropping by to chat, collect rent or look around.

### What the notice must say

| Required | What it means |
|---|---|
| In writing | A text or verbal heads-up alone isn't notice (see below for email) |
| At least 24 hours before | Counted from when you're considered to have received it |
| The reason | Specific is better: "replace kitchen faucet", not "maintenance" |
| The date | The day of entry |
| A time between 8 a.m. and 8 p.m. | A specific time, or a reasonable window |

The LTB's guideline says a window is fine when the landlord doesn't control the schedule, for example when a cable company gives a three-hour slot. In *Wrona v. Toronto Community Housing Corporation*, the Divisional Court found that a **nine-hour** window for smoke alarm checks didn't meet the rule.

### How the notice has to reach you

The notice must be delivered in a way the LTB accepts, and the method affects when the 24 hours start.

| Method | When it counts as received |
|---|---|
| Handed to you | The same day |
| Left in your mailbox | The same day |
| Courier | The next day that isn't a holiday |
| Email | The day it's sent, **only if you agreed in writing** to accept notices by email (for example, in your standard lease) |
| Regular mail | Five days after mailing |

Landlords can also slide the notice under your door, put it through your mail slot or give it to an apparent adult in your unit. A notice mailed on Monday for entry on Tuesday doesn't work.

## Entry without written notice

The RTA allows entry **without** written notice in four situations:

- **Emergencies,** such as a fire, flood or gas leak.
- **You consent at the time.** If the landlord knocks and you say "come in", that's valid. Agreeing yesterday by phone isn't the same as written notice.
- **Regular cleaning** that your lease says the landlord provides, at the times in the lease or, if none are listed, between 8 a.m. and 8 p.m.
- **Showings to prospective tenants** once you and the landlord have agreed to end the tenancy or either of you has given notice. The landlord must come between 8 a.m. and 8 p.m. and, before entering, tell you or make a reasonable effort to tell you.

That last one matters if you've given an N9 to move out or received an N12 or N13. Showings to new tenants can happen without 24 hours' written notice, but the time limits and the effort to warn you still apply. If you're on your way out, our guides to [ending a tenancy with an N9](/blog/ending-a-tenancy-n9/) and [N12 and N13 evictions](/blog/n12-n13-eviction-ontario/) explain the rest of the process.

### A common trap: repairs you asked for

Even if you reported the leak, the landlord **can't just walk in** to fix it. The LTB's guideline says they still need written notice, or your consent at the time they arrive.

## Your responsibilities during a valid entry

The rules work both ways. When the notice is proper:

- **Don't block or delay it.** The LTB says you can't refuse just because the time is inconvenient, and the Ontario government lists stopping a properly noticed entry as an offence. You can always ask for a different time; many landlords will agree.
- **Make the work area reachable,** and safely secure pets.
- **Don't change the locks** without the landlord's consent. That's also an offence.

You're allowed to stay in the unit during the entry. The landlord can also enter if you're out, as long as the notice was valid.

## When entries become harassment

Even valid entries can cross a line. The LTB expects landlords to limit entries to what's actually needed for the work or inspection. If entries are unnecessary or unreasonably frequent, the Board may find the landlord harassed you or **substantially interfered with your reasonable enjoyment** of your home.

Signs worth documenting:

- Inspections every week with vague reasons
- Notices that always list a full-day window
- Entries that seem timed to pressure you to move
- Staff or contractors entering without the landlord or superintendent present (the LTB says the landlord or super should normally attend)

## What to do if your landlord breaks the rules

### 1. Write it down

Keep a log with dates, times, who entered, what they did and whether you were home. Save photos, video from a door camera you own, texts and emails. Note anyone who saw it.

### 2. Put your concern in writing

A short, calm message works: "On November 3 at 2 p.m. you entered my unit without written notice. Please give me 24 hours' written notice, with the reason and time, before any future non-emergency entry, as required by sections 26 and 27 of the Residential Tenancies Act."

### 3. File a T2 at the LTB

**Form T2 (Application about Tenant Rights)** covers illegal entry, harassment and substantial interference.

- **Deadline:** within one year of what happened
- **Fee:** $53, or $48 on the Tribunals Ontario Portal (a fee waiver is available if you qualify)

If the Board agrees, it can:

- order the landlord to stop
- order a rent abatement
- order the landlord to pay your reasonable out-of-pocket costs and for damaged property
- order the landlord to pay an administrative fine to the Board
- end the tenancy, or make any other order it considers appropriate

Our step-by-step guide to [LTB tenant applications](/blog/ltb-tenant-applications/) covers evidence, hearings and free legal help.

### 4. Report the offence

Entering for a reason the RTA doesn't allow, without the required notice, or outside the allowed hours is an **offence** under section 234 of the Act. You can contact the province's **Rental Housing Enforcement Unit**, which investigates and can prosecute. Maximum fines are now $100,000 for individuals and $500,000 for corporations.

## Valid-notice checklist

- [ ] In writing, delivered by an accepted method
- [ ] Received at least 24 hours before entry
- [ ] States a reason the RTA allows
- [ ] Gives the date
- [ ] Gives a time, or a reasonable window, between 8 a.m. and 8 p.m.

If any box is empty and there's no emergency, you can politely say no and ask for a proper notice.

## Bottom line

Your landlord has a right to enter for real reasons, and you have a right to know when and why. Most issues are solved with one clear written message. When they aren't, a T2 at the LTB and a report to the Rental Housing Enforcement Unit are there to back you up.

## FAQ

**Can my landlord enter without 24 hours' notice in Ontario?**
Only in a few situations: an emergency, when you agree to the entry at the time, regular cleaning that your lease says the landlord provides, or showing the unit to prospective tenants after a notice to end the tenancy has been given or agreed. Showings must be between 8 a.m. and 8 p.m., after the landlord tries to let you know.

**What does a valid notice of entry need to say?**
It must be in writing, given at least 24 hours before the entry, and state the reason for entry, the date and a time of entry between 8 a.m. and 8 p.m. A specific time is best. A reasonable window is allowed when the landlord doesn't control the schedule, but a court found a nine-hour window too broad.

**Can I refuse entry if the time is inconvenient?**
Not if the notice is valid. The LTB says a tenant can't deny entry just because the time is inconvenient, and stopping a properly noticed entry is an offence under the Residential Tenancies Act. You can ask politely for another time, and you can stay in the unit while the landlord is there.

**What can I do if my landlord keeps entering illegally?**
Keep a dated log, photos or video, and copies of messages, then tell the landlord in writing to follow the notice rules. If it continues, file a Form T2 with the Landlord and Tenant Board within one year. The Board can order a rent abatement, an administrative fine and other remedies. Illegal entry can also be reported to the Rental Housing Enforcement Unit.

## Sources

- [Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, sections 26, 27 and 234 (Ontario e-Laws)](https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/06r17)
- [LTB Interpretation Guideline 19: The Landlord's Right of Entry](https://tribunalsontario.ca/documents/ltb/Interpretation%20Guidelines/19%20-%20The%20Landlords%20Right%20of%20Entry%20into%20a%20Rental%20Unit.html)
- [LTB Brochure: How to Serve a Landlord or Tenant with Documents](https://tribunalsontario.ca/documents/ltb/Brochures/How%20to%20Serve%20a%20Landlord%20or%20Tenant%20with%20Documents.html)
- [LTB: Application and hearing process](https://tribunalsontario.ca/ltb/application-and-hearing-process/)
- [Government of Ontario: Rental housing offences](https://www.ontario.ca/page/rental-housing-offences)
- [Government of Ontario: Renting in Ontario, your rights](https://www.ontario.ca/page/renting-ontario-your-rights)

# Landlord Repairs Ontario: What They Must Fix and What to Do

URL: https://www.colivease.ca/blog/landlord-repairs-ontario/
Language: English
Updated: 2026-11-03

Landlord repairs in Ontario: what your landlord must fix, how to ask in writing, Toronto 311 and RentSafeTO timelines, the T6 form and why not to withhold rent.

In Ontario, your landlord must keep your unit and building in a good state of repair, fit to live in, and up to health, safety, housing and maintenance standards, even if the problem was there when you moved in. Ask for repairs in writing, give the landlord a reasonable time to act, and if nothing happens, call your city (311 in Toronto) and file a Form T6 maintenance application with the Landlord and Tenant Board (LTB). Don't stop paying rent: that can put your tenancy at risk.

Here's what counts as the landlord's job, how to make a request that holds up later, and what to do when repairs stall.

## Key takeaways

- **Repairs are the landlord's legal duty** under section 20 of the Residential Tenancies Act (RTA), and a lease can't take that away.
- **It applies even to problems you saw before signing.**
- **You're responsible** for ordinary cleanliness and for damage you, your guests or people living with you cause beyond normal wear and tear.
- **Put every request in writing** and keep copies, photos and dates.
- **Toronto:** RentSafeTO buildings must answer urgent requests within 24 hours and others within seven days. Unresolved problems go to 311.
- **The LTB route is Form T6**, filed within one year. The fee is $53, or $48 on the Tribunals Ontario Portal.
- **Never withhold rent** without the Board's permission.

*This article is general information, not legal advice. For your situation, contact the [Landlord and Tenant Board](https://tribunalsontario.ca/ltb/) or a community legal clinic (Legal Aid Ontario can refer you to one at 1-800-668-8258).*

## Does the RTA cover your rental?

The RTA covers most private rentals in Ontario: apartments, condos, houses, basement units and rooms in rooming houses. The big exception is when you **share a kitchen or bathroom with the owner** (or certain close family members of the owner) who lives there. In that case the RTA generally doesn't apply, the LTB can't hear a repair case, and you rely on your written agreement and city property standards instead. Our guide to [living with your landlord in Ontario](/blog/living-with-your-landlord-ontario/) explains how that works.

## What your landlord must repair and maintain

The LTB's maintenance brochure lists what this covers in practice. If the landlord provides it, the landlord keeps it working:

- Plumbing, electrical and heating systems
- Appliances that came with the unit, such as the fridge, stove or washer
- Walls, ceilings, roofs and carpets
- Windows, doors, locks and lighting
- Common areas: lobby, halls, elevators, laundry room, parking and walkways
- Pest control for problems like cockroaches and mice
- Cleanliness of shared areas

If something wears out or breaks through normal use, the landlord repairs or replaces it. A replacement doesn't have to be new or fancier, but it must work properly.

### Vital services and heat

Landlords can't withhold **vital services**: hot or cold water, fuel, electricity, gas and, during the heating season, heat. That's true even if rent is late. Doing it on purpose is an offence under the RTA.

Heat standards depend on where you live:

| Rule | Minimum | Period |
|---|---|---|
| Provincial standard (where the landlord supplies heat) | 20°C | September 1 to June 15 |
| City of Toronto bylaw (where heat is at the landlord's expense) | 21°C | October 1 to May 15 |
| Toronto, if the landlord provides air conditioning | No more than 26°C | June 1 to September 30 |

Where a municipal standard is higher, the higher one applies.

### What's on you as the tenant

- Keep the unit reasonably clean.
- Repair or pay for **undue damage** you, a guest or someone living with you causes, whether on purpose or by carelessness.
- Report problems promptly. A small leak you never mention can become a much bigger argument later.

Normal wear and tear, like a carpet that thins after years of use, is not your responsibility.

## How to request repairs in writing

Email or a text message both work, as long as you can show it was sent. Keep it short and factual.

**What to include:**

1. Your name, address and unit number
2. What's wrong, where, and when it started
3. Photos or a short video, with dates
4. How it affects you ("no hot water in the kitchen or bathroom")
5. A clear ask and a reasonable date ("Please arrange repairs by Friday, November 14")
6. When you're available for access, so the landlord can give proper notice

Keep a simple log: dates you reported the issue, every reply, every visit and whether the work was done. If the landlord sends a tradesperson, they still need to give you **24 hours' written notice** for non-emergency work, unless you agree at the time. Our guide to [landlord entry rules in Ontario](/blog/landlord-entry-rules-ontario/) covers this in detail.

## How long should repairs take?

The RTA doesn't set one deadline for every repair. The standard is a **reasonable time**, which depends on how urgent the problem is. No heat in January is not the same as a sticky cupboard door.

Toronto's RentSafeTO program gives firmer timelines for apartment buildings with **three or more storeys and 10 or more units**:

| Type of request | Landlord must respond within |
|---|---|
| Urgent: heat, water, electricity, gas, building security | 24 hours |
| Non-urgent: everything else | 7 days |

RentSafeTO landlords must also track service requests and keep copies for 24 months, and you can ask to see your records. Condos, townhomes and units in a private house (like a basement apartment) are not part of RentSafeTO, but city property standards still apply to them.

## If nothing happens: your options

### 1. Follow up in writing

Send one more message that refers to your first request and gives a final date. It shows you gave the landlord a fair chance.

### 2. Call your city

In Toronto, contact **311** by phone or through the 311 app. A bylaw enforcement officer will follow up, may ask for photos and a copy of your request to the landlord, and can issue a Notice of Violation or Order to Comply. The City aims to respond to urgent complaints within 24 hours and non-urgent ones within 5 to 10 days. If the landlord still doesn't comply, the City can lay charges, or do the work itself and add the cost to the owner's property tax bill.

Outside Toronto, contact your municipality's property standards or bylaw office.

### 3. File a T6 at the Landlord and Tenant Board

**Form T6 (Tenant Application about Maintenance)** is filed through the Tribunals Ontario Portal.

- **Deadline:** within one year of the problem
- **Fee:** $53, or $48 online (low-income tenants can ask for a fee waiver)
- **Evidence:** photos, your written requests, your log, any city work orders

The Board can:

- order the landlord to make repairs by a set date
- order a **rent abatement** (a partial refund or reduction)
- let you make the repair and have the landlord repay you
- order the landlord to pay for your damaged belongings and other reasonable out-of-pocket costs
- stop the landlord from raising your rent until serious problems are fixed
- end the tenancy, if that's what you want

If the landlord's agent or superintendent is also harassing you or cutting off services, that's a separate **Form T2** issue. Our walkthrough of [LTB tenant applications](/blog/ltb-tenant-applications/) explains filing, fees, fee waivers and hearings step by step.

## Why you must not withhold rent

It's tempting to hold back rent until the landlord acts. The LTB is clear that you shouldn't, and the 2026 changes make it riskier:

- **Late rent opens the door to eviction.** Your landlord can serve an N4 notice, and for notices given on or after September 21, 2026, the notice period is just **7 days**.
- **Raising repairs at a rent hearing now costs money up front.** If your landlord files a rent arrears application on or after September 21, 2026, you must pay the landlord at least **half of the arrears claimed**, at least seven days before the hearing, before you can raise maintenance issues there.

The safer option is built into the T6 process: you can file a **Request to Pay Rent to the Board** with your application. If the Board agrees, you pay your rent to the LTB, not the landlord, until your case is decided. You stay up to date on rent, and the landlord can see the money is waiting.

## Repairs when you rent with roommates

If you and your roommates are all on the lease, any of you can report the problem, but agree on one person to send the written requests so the record is clear. Repairs for damage a roommate caused are a matter between you; the LTB doesn't settle roommate disputes. A written [roommate agreement](/blog/roommate-agreement-ontario/) that covers damage and cleaning saves a lot of stress here.

## Repair request checklist

- [ ] Problem reported in writing, with photos and dates
- [ ] Reasonable deadline given, plus your availability for access
- [ ] Log of every reply, visit and missed deadline
- [ ] Follow-up message sent
- [ ] 311 (or your city) contacted if repairs still stall
- [ ] T6 filed within one year, with a Request to Pay Rent to the Board if needed
- [ ] Rent paid in full and on time throughout

## Bottom line

Repairs are your landlord's job, not a favour. Keep everything in writing, use 311 and RentSafeTO in Toronto to put pressure on, and take it to the LTB with a T6 if you have to. Keep paying rent the whole time so your own tenancy is never the thing in question.

## FAQ

**Does my Ontario landlord have to fix things that were broken when I moved in?**
Yes. Under section 20 of the Residential Tenancies Act, the landlord must keep the unit in a good state of repair and meet health, safety, housing and maintenance standards, even if you knew about the problem before you signed. Report it in writing and keep a copy, just as you would for something that broke later.

**How long does a landlord have to make repairs in Ontario?**
The Residential Tenancies Act says repairs must be made within a reasonable time, which depends on how serious the problem is. In Toronto apartment buildings covered by RentSafeTO, landlords must respond to urgent requests about heat, water, electricity, gas or building security within 24 hours, and to other requests within seven days.

**Can I stop paying rent until my landlord fixes something?**
No. The Landlord and Tenant Board warns tenants not to withhold rent, even when repairs are overdue. Your landlord could serve an N4 notice and apply to evict you. Instead, file a T6 maintenance application and, if you want, ask the Board for permission to pay your rent to the Board until your case is decided.

**What can the Landlord and Tenant Board order on a T6 application?**
The Board can order the landlord to do the repairs by a deadline, reduce your rent through an abatement, repay you for reasonable repair costs or damaged belongings, stop rent increases until serious problems are fixed, or end the tenancy. You must file within one year of the problem, and the fee is $53, or $48 on the Tribunals Ontario Portal.

**Who do I call in Toronto if my landlord won't fix my apartment?**
After asking your landlord in writing, contact 311 by phone or the 311 app to open a service request. A City bylaw officer can inspect and order the landlord to comply. In buildings with three or more storeys and 10 or more units, the RentSafeTO program sets response timelines your landlord must meet.

## Sources

- [Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (Ontario e-Laws)](https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/06r17)
- [LTB Brochure: Maintenance and Repairs](https://tribunalsontario.ca/documents/ltb/Brochures/Maintenance%20and%20Repairs.html)
- [LTB: Forms, filing and fees](https://tribunalsontario.ca/ltb/forms-filing-and-fees/)
- [LTB Operational Update: Legislative changes effective September 21, 2026](https://tribunalsontario.ca/2026/09/21/ltb-operational-update-legislative-changes-at-the-landlord-and-tenant-board-effective-september-21-2026/)
- [City of Toronto: RentSafeTO service requests, complaints and investigations](https://www.toronto.ca/community-people/housing-shelter/rental-housing-rights-information/housing-property-standards/apartment-building-standards/rentsafeto-for-tenants/rentsafeto-for-tenants-service-requests-complaints-investigations/)
- [City of Toronto: Indoor temperatures in apartment units](https://www.toronto.ca/community-people/housing-shelter/rental-housing-rights-information/housing-property-standards/indoor-temperatures-in-apartment-units/)
- [Government of Ontario: Rental housing offences](https://www.ontario.ca/page/rental-housing-offences)

# LTB Tenant Applications: How to File a T2, T6, T1 or T5

URL: https://www.colivease.ca/blog/ltb-tenant-applications/
Language: English
Updated: 2026-11-03

How to file a tenant application at the Landlord and Tenant Board: T1, T2, T5 and T6 forms, fees and waivers, the Tribunals Ontario Portal, hearings and help.

To take a landlord to Ontario's Landlord and Tenant Board (LTB), pick the right tenant form (T2 for tenant rights like illegal entry or harassment, T6 for repairs, T1 for money owed back, T5 for bad-faith evictions), file it on the Tribunals Ontario Portal, and pay $48 online (or $53 by other methods), unless you qualify for a fee waiver. The LTB then schedules mediation or a hearing, usually by Zoom or phone, where you present your evidence.

You don't need a lawyer to file, and free help is available. Here's the whole process, start to finish.

## Key takeaways

- **Most tenant problems fit one of four forms:** T1, T2, T5 or T6.
- **Deadlines are short:** generally one year for T1, T2, T6 and most T5s.
- **Fees:** $53, or $48 on the Tribunals Ontario Portal. Low-income tenants can ask for a waiver.
- **Hearings are mostly virtual,** by Zoom or phone.
- **Evidence must be shared in advance:** at least 7 days before the hearing (5 for responding evidence).
- **Free help:** community legal clinics, Tenant Duty Counsel, and the LTB's own phone line and online tool.

*This article is general information, not legal advice. For your situation, contact the [Landlord and Tenant Board](https://tribunalsontario.ca/ltb/) or a community legal clinic (Legal Aid Ontario can refer you to one at 1-800-668-8258).*

## Before you file: can the LTB help?

The LTB handles disputes between landlords and tenants under the Residential Tenancies Act (RTA). It **can't** help with:

- **Disputes with roommates.** If you're co-tenants, you work it out yourselves or go to Small Claims Court. Our guide to [dealing with a bad roommate](/blog/dealing-with-a-bad-roommate/) covers your options.
- **Rentals where you share a kitchen or bathroom with the owner** who lives there. The RTA usually doesn't apply. See [living with your landlord in Ontario](/blog/living-with-your-landlord-ontario/).
- **Most problems before a lease begins,** with one exception: if you signed a lease and paid a rent deposit but the landlord didn't let you move in, you can file a T1 to get the deposit back.

It also helps to try a written request first. It's often the fastest fix, and it becomes evidence if you do file.

## Which form do you need?

| Form | Use it for | Deadline |
|---|---|---|
| **T1** Tenant Application for a Rebate | Money a landlord collected or kept illegally: illegal deposits or fees, unpaid deposit interest, rent above the legal amount, unpaid N12/N13 compensation | 1 year after the money was collected or kept |
| **T2** Application about Tenant Rights | Illegal entry, harassment, threats, substantial interference, withheld vital services, lockouts without new keys | 1 year after the conduct |
| **T5** Landlord Gave a Notice of Termination in Bad Faith | Landlord or buyer didn't move in, or the renovation or demolition never happened; refusal of your right to move back after renovations | 1 year after you moved out (refusal to let you return: later of 2 years after moving out or 6 months after the work ended) |
| **T6** Tenant Application about Maintenance | Repairs and maintenance the landlord hasn't done | 1 year after the problem |
| **T3** Rent Reduction | Rent reduction when services drop or property taxes fall | See the form instructions (filed by mail, email or at ServiceOntario) |
| **A2** Sublet or Assignment | Disputes about subletting or assigning your lease | See the form instructions (filed by mail, email or at ServiceOntario) |

You can combine issues: a single situation might involve a T6 for the broken heating and a T2 for the superintendent's harassment. For specific problems, see our guides to [landlord repairs](/blog/landlord-repairs-ontario/), [landlord entry rules](/blog/landlord-entry-rules-ontario/) and [N12 and N13 evictions](/blog/n12-n13-eviction-ontario/).

## Fees and fee waivers

| Application | Fee |
|---|---|
| T1, T2, T5, T6 | $53, or **$48** on the Tribunals Ontario Portal |
| T3, T4, T7, A1, A2, A4 | $53 |
| Multi-tenant application | $53 for the first unit + $5 per extra unit, up to $450 (mail or courier only) |
| Request to review an order | $58 |

LTB fees are **non-refundable**, so check your form carefully.

### Fee waivers

You can ask the LTB to waive fees if you're an individual and either:

- your household's main income is from Ontario Works, ODSP, Old Age Security **with** the Guaranteed Income Supplement, War Veterans Allowance or the Canada Pension Plan, or
- your gross monthly household income is below the LTB's limit for your household size (the limits are set out with the Fee Waiver Request form and the LTB's fee waiver practice direction).

Complete the **Fee Waiver Request** form and file it with your application. The LTB may ask for financial documents. Asking costs nothing, and once a waiver is granted, it covers the LTB's fees for that application from then on.

## How to file

### On the Tribunals Ontario Portal (recommended)

You can file T1, T2, T5 and T6 applications online:

1. Create or sign in to your Tribunals Ontario Portal account.
2. Follow the step-by-step application.
3. Pay the fee online by card.
4. Use the portal to check your file, upload evidence, message the other party and try the online dispute resolution tool.

### Other ways to file

- **By mail or courier** to the LTB at 15 Grosvenor Street, Ground Floor, Toronto, ON M7A 2G6, with payment as described in the form instructions (the LTB has a Credit Card Payment Form for this).
- **In person** at a ServiceOntario location that accepts LTB documents. ServiceOntario staff can't give legal or procedural advice.
- **By email** for some forms, including T3, T7, A1 and A2, after paying online.

Whatever the method, the form must be complete. LTB staff check applications, and mistakes can lead to refusal or dismissal.

## After you file: mediation and hearings

The LTB usually sends both sides the application and a **notice of hearing** with the date, time and format. Sometimes it orders you to serve the documents yourself; if so, follow the instructions exactly.

### Try to settle

On the portal, the **online dispute resolution** tool lets you and your landlord negotiate. A **Dispute Resolution Officer** can help, and if you reach a deal it can become a consent order or a mediated agreement. Mediation is voluntary: if it doesn't work, you go to a hearing.

### The hearing

- **Format:** most hearings are by **Zoom** video or phone. Written hearings are possible, and in-person hearings happen only for approved accommodation requests.
- **Arrive early:** log on or call in at least 15 minutes before. If you're not there when your case is called, it can proceed without you.
- **The adjudicator is neutral** and can't give you legal advice. It's up to you to explain your case and show your evidence.
- **You can bring a support person,** or a representative who speaks for you.
- **Language:** hearings run in English or French, and you can ask for a sign language interpreter as an accommodation. For other languages, you usually need to bring your own interpreter, such as a bilingual friend or a professional.

## Evidence that wins cases

Evidence can be documents, photos, videos, emails, texts and social media posts. The adjudicator decides what's accepted.

- **Deadline:** give all your evidence to the landlord and the LTB at least **7 days** before the hearing, or 5 days for responding evidence, unless the LTB says otherwise. Under the LTB's Rules, these are calendar days.
- **Upload it** on the portal for portal applications, and serve the other side too, unless they've agreed in writing to receive it through the portal.
- **Organize it:** a dated timeline, your written requests, the landlord's replies, photos, receipts, city work orders and witness names.
- **Witnesses:** if someone won't come voluntarily, you can request a summons, but you'll have to pay witness fees.

## After the hearing

You'll get a written **order**. You can ask for written reasons at the hearing or within 30 days. If you think there was a serious error, you can **request a review within 15 days** (shortened from 30 on July 1, 2026; fee $58). An appeal to the Divisional Court must be filed within 30 days and only on a question of law.

## If your landlord files against you

If your landlord applies to evict you for unpaid rent, you can raise maintenance or tenant-rights issues at that hearing, but under rules that took effect September 21, 2026, you must give the landlord and the LTB a written description of the issues (and your evidence) at least 7 days before the hearing and, for applications filed on or after that date, pay the landlord at least half of the arrears claimed at least 7 days before the hearing. Get advice early.

## Where to get free help

- **Community legal clinics:** free advice and sometimes representation for low-income tenants. Call Legal Aid Ontario at **1-800-668-8258** (416-979-1446 in the GTA).
- **Tenant Duty Counsel Program:** run by ACTO and funded by Legal Aid Ontario, it gives unrepresented tenants remote advice on or before their hearing day, with priority for eviction cases.
- **Federation of Metro Tenants' Associations** (Toronto) tenant hotline: **416-921-9494**.
- **The LTB:** 416-645-8080 or 1-888-332-3234, plus **Navigate Tribunals Ontario**, its free online tool.
- **Steps to Justice:** plain-language legal information for Ontario.

## Filing checklist

- [ ] Problem reported to the landlord in writing first
- [ ] Right form chosen, within the deadline
- [ ] Fee paid, or a Fee Waiver Request attached
- [ ] Timeline and evidence organized and shared at least 7 days ahead
- [ ] Hearing link tested, joining 15 minutes early
- [ ] Legal clinic or Tenant Duty Counsel contacted

## Bottom line

The LTB is built for people without lawyers. Pick the right form, file on time, organize your evidence, and lean on free help like legal clinics and Tenant Duty Counsel. Most tenant applications cost $48 online, and nothing at all if you qualify for a fee waiver.

## FAQ

**How much does it cost to file a tenant application at the LTB?**
Forms T1, T2, T5 and T6 cost $53, or $48 if you file on the Tribunals Ontario Portal. T3, T4, T7, A1, A2 and A4 cost $53. A multi-tenant application costs $53 for the first unit plus $5 for each additional unit, up to $450. LTB fees aren't refundable, but low-income tenants can ask for a fee waiver.

**Who qualifies for an LTB fee waiver?**
Individuals whose main household income comes from Ontario Works, the Ontario Disability Support Program, Old Age Security with the Guaranteed Income Supplement, War Veterans Allowance or the Canada Pension Plan, or whose gross monthly household income is below the LTB's limit for their household size. Asking is free, and you file the Fee Waiver Request form with your application.

**How long do I have to file a T2 or T6?**
Generally one year from the conduct or problem you're complaining about. A T1 for money a landlord collected or kept illegally also has a one-year limit. A T5 about a bad-faith N12 or N13 must be filed within one year of moving out, with a longer deadline if a landlord refused your right to move back after renovations.

**Are LTB hearings in person?**
Usually not. Most LTB mediations and hearings happen by Zoom video or phone, and in-person hearings are scheduled only for approved accommodation requests. Join at least 15 minutes early. If you aren't there when your case is called, the hearing can go ahead without you, and your application could be dismissed.

**Where can I get free legal help for an LTB hearing?**
Low-income tenants can contact a community legal clinic through Legal Aid Ontario at 1-800-668-8258. The Tenant Duty Counsel Program, run by ACTO and funded by Legal Aid Ontario, gives free advice to unrepresented tenants on or before their hearing day. In Toronto, the Federation of Metro Tenants' Associations hotline is 416-921-9494.

## Sources

- [LTB: Forms, filing and fees](https://tribunalsontario.ca/ltb/forms-filing-and-fees/)
- [LTB: Application and hearing process](https://tribunalsontario.ca/ltb/application-and-hearing-process/)
- [LTB Practice Direction on Fee Waiver](https://tribunalsontario.ca/documents/ltb/Practice%20Directions/Practice%20Direction%20on%20Fee%20Waiver%20(Jan%2016%202017).html)
- [Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, sections 29, 57, 135 and 210 (Ontario e-Laws)](https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/06r17)
- [LTB Operational Update: Legislative changes effective July 1, 2026](https://tribunalsontario.ca/2026/06/30/ltb-operational-update-legislative-changes-at-the-ltb/)
- [LTB Operational Update: Legislative changes effective September 21, 2026](https://tribunalsontario.ca/2026/09/21/ltb-operational-update-legislative-changes-at-the-landlord-and-tenant-board-effective-september-21-2026/)
- [ACTO: Tenant Duty Counsel Program](https://www.acto.ca/for-tenants/tenant-duty-counsel/)
- [Government of Ontario: Renting in Ontario, your rights](https://www.ontario.ca/page/renting-ontario-your-rights)

# Moving Out Checklist Ontario: Notice, Cleaning and Deposits

URL: https://www.colivease.ca/blog/moving-out-checklist-ontario/
Language: English
Updated: 2026-11-03

Moving out in Ontario: N9 notice timing, ending early with an N11, cleaning, a photo walkthrough, utilities, address changes, deposits and roommate handovers.

To move out of a rental in Ontario, give your landlord at least **60 days' written notice on Form N9**, ending on the last day of a rental period (and not before the end of a fixed term), or sign an **N11** agreement to end the tenancy on a date you both accept. Then leave the unit reasonably clean, take everything with you, document it with photos, return your keys and let your **last month's rent deposit** cover your final month.

Use the timeline below so nothing slips, especially if roommates are staying behind.

## Key takeaways

- **Notice:** N9, at least 60 days for monthly and fixed-term tenancies, 28 days for daily or weekly. Add 5 days if mailing.
- **Termination date:** the last day of a rental period, and not before the end of a fixed term.
- **Leaving early:** agree with your landlord (N11) or assign your lease. A landlord can't force you to sign an N11.
- **Clean, don't renovate:** ordinary cleanliness, plus repairing damage you or guests caused.
- **Take everything.** Items left behind after you move out can be disposed of.
- **Your deposit covers your last month**, plus interest owed.

*This is general information, not legal advice. For your situation, contact the [Landlord and Tenant Board](https://tribunalsontario.ca/ltb/) or a community legal clinic through Legal Aid Ontario or Steps to Justice.*

## Step 1: Give proper notice (N9)

Use the LTB's **Form N9: Tenant's Notice to End the Tenancy**. A text saying "we're moving" is risky; the form makes the date and your intention clear.

| Your tenancy | Minimum notice | Termination date must be |
|---|---|---|
| Monthly (no fixed term) | 60 days | The last day of a rental month |
| Fixed term (e.g., one-year lease) | 60 days | Not earlier than the last day of the term |
| Daily or weekly | 28 days | The last day of a rental week |

A few rules people miss:

- **Notice is needed even at the end of a lease.** A fixed-term lease doesn't end by itself; it rolls into a monthly tenancy.
- **Don't count the day you deliver the notice.** If you mail it, add 5 days (65 instead of 60).
- **February and March:** notice for the end of February is fine if given by January 1, and for the end of March by February 1.
- **If your landlord gave you an N12 or N13**, you can give an N9 with as little as 10 days' notice, and the date doesn't have to be the end of a rental period.
- **If you leave without proper notice**, you may owe rent until the unit is re-rented or until the earliest date proper notice would have ended the tenancy, whichever comes first.

Our full guide to [ending a tenancy with Form N9](/blog/ending-a-tenancy-n9/) has worked examples.

## Step 2: Need out sooner? Agree to end it (N11) or assign

If 60 days or the end of your term doesn't work, you have options:

- **Agreement to end the tenancy (Form N11).** You and your landlord can agree to end the tenancy on any date. A verbal agreement can count, but a signed N11 avoids confusion. Keep a copy.
- **Assignment.** With your landlord's consent, someone new takes over your lease on the same terms. If the landlord refuses to allow any assignment, or doesn't reply within seven days of your request, you can give an N9 within 30 days of your request, with at least 30 days' notice. See [sublets and assignments in Ontario](/blog/sublet-and-assignment-ontario/).

Know the limits:

- **A landlord can't force you** to sign an N11, and can't make signing an N9 or N11 a condition of renting the unit in the first place (some student housing is an exception).
- **Once you've signed or given notice, it binds you.** If you don't leave, the landlord can apply to the LTB to evict you. As of September 21, 2026, if the LTB issues an eviction order without a hearing based on your N9 or N11, it can only cancel that order if doing so wouldn't be unfair, and it can't consider changes in your circumstances after you signed. Be sure before you commit.

## Step 3: Prepare the unit

Once notice is given, your landlord may start showing the unit. Our sibling guide to [landlord entry rules in Ontario](/blog/landlord-entry-rules-ontario/) explains when they can come in.

**Cleaning.** Tenants must keep the unit at a standard of ordinary cleanliness, and repair damage caused by them or their guests, whether on purpose or through carelessness. Normal wear and tear, like aging paint, worn carpet or a tired stove element, is the landlord's responsibility. A landlord can't take a cleaning deposit or keep your rent deposit for cleaning.

A practical cleaning list:

- [ ] Kitchen: inside the fridge, oven and cabinets; wipe counters and the range hood
- [ ] Bathroom: toilet, tub, sink, mirror and floor
- [ ] Floors swept and mopped or vacuumed
- [ ] Nail holes: ask your landlord how they'd like small holes handled
- [ ] Remove all garbage, recycling and furniture you own
- [ ] Return anything the landlord provided to where it was

## Step 4: Do a move-out walkthrough with photos

There's no legal requirement for a joint inspection, but it's the best protection you have.

1. **Invite your landlord** to walk through with you on your last day or shortly before.
2. **Take dated photos and video** of every room, inside appliances and closets, walls, floors and any existing damage. Compare with your move-in photos.
3. **Note meter readings** if you pay hydro or gas.
4. **Write down anything agreed**, like "landlord accepts unit as clean", and ask them to confirm by email.
5. **Return all keys and fobs** and get written confirmation, so your key deposit comes back.

**Take everything with you.** If you move out after giving an N9 or signing an N11, you lose your rights to anything left behind, and the landlord can keep, sell or throw it out right away.

## Step 5: Utilities, insurance and address changes

| When | Task |
|---|---|
| 3–4 weeks before | Book movers or a truck; ask your new building about elevator bookings |
| 2–3 weeks before | Schedule end-of-service for hydro, gas, internet and anything else in your name. See our sibling guide to [utilities for renters in Toronto](/blog/utilities-for-renters-toronto/) |
| 2 weeks before | Move your tenant insurance to the new address, effective on move day |
| 1 week before | Set up mail forwarding with Canada Post if you need it |
| Within 6 days of moving | Update your Ontario driver's licence and vehicle permit (legally required) |
| Within 30 days of moving | Update your health card address |
| Soon after | Update your address with the Canada Revenue Agency, your bank, employer, school and phone carrier |

ServiceOntario lets you update your driver's licence, health card and photo card together online, except health cards with an address printed on them, which must be updated in person.

## Step 6: Your last month's rent and other money

- **Let the deposit cover your last month.** A rent deposit can only be used for your final rent period. Tell your landlord in writing to apply the deposit, plus any interest owed, to your last month. If it's not enough, pay the difference.
- **Don't pay twice.** If the landlord asks for full rent for your last month while holding your deposit, point to the deposit in writing.
- **Key deposit:** refundable when you return all keys and fobs.
- **Receipts:** you can ask for a rent receipt for up to 12 months after you move out.
- **If money isn't returned**, ask in writing first. You can then contact the Rental Housing Enforcement Unit (1-888-772-9277) or apply to the LTB with Form T1. More detail in our guide to [rent deposit rules in Ontario](/blog/rent-deposit-rules-ontario/).

A landlord who says you still owe money after you've moved out generally has to apply to the LTB within one year of your move-out date, so keep your photos, receipts and messages for at least that long.

## Roommate handovers

Shared homes need a plan for who leaves, who stays and how money moves.

- **Everyone on the lease is responsible for the full rent**, not just their share, until the tenancy ends or the landlord agrees otherwise.
- **The N9 asks for all tenant names.** If only one co-tenant is leaving, how that notice affects everyone else isn't always straightforward. Talk to the landlord and your roommates first, and get the outcome in writing, such as an assignment of the departing person's spot or a new lease for those staying. A legal clinic can help if it gets complicated.
- **Settle the deposit.** The landlord usually holds a single rent deposit for the whole unit. If you're leaving and someone is replacing you, agree in writing that the newcomer pays you your share and takes over your portion of the deposit.
- **Transfer shared accounts.** Move any utility or internet account in your name to someone staying, and agree on the final bill split.
- **Divide shared items** you bought together, and agree who keeps what.
- **If your roommate rents a room from you** rather than from the landlord, your [roommate agreement](/blog/roommate-agreement-ontario/) sets the notice you owe each other. And if you share a kitchen or bathroom with the owner, the Residential Tenancies Act may not apply at all; see [living with your landlord](/blog/living-with-your-landlord-ontario/).

## Bottom line

Give the right notice on the right form, then treat move-out like a handover: clean, photograph, return keys and put every agreement in writing. Your last month's rent deposit should cover your final month, and good records make any dispute short.

## FAQ

**How much notice do I need to give before moving out in Ontario?**
For monthly and fixed-term tenancies, give at least 60 days' written notice using Form N9, with a termination date on the last day of a rental period. In a fixed-term lease it can't be earlier than the end of the term. Daily or weekly tenancies need 28 days. Add 5 days if you mail the notice.

**Can I move out before my lease ends in Ontario?**
Yes, if your landlord agrees. You can sign an agreement to end the tenancy on any date you both accept, ideally on Form N11. Other options include assigning your lease to a new tenant with the landlord's consent. If you just leave without proper notice, you may owe rent until the unit is re-rented or the earliest date proper notice would have allowed.

**Do I have to clean before moving out?**
You must leave the unit at the standard of ordinary cleanliness and repair any damage you or your guests caused beyond normal wear and tear. Your landlord can't charge a cleaning deposit or keep your last month's rent deposit for cleaning or damage. Photos of the clean, empty unit protect you if there's a dispute later.

**What happens to things I leave behind after moving out?**
If you move out after giving an N9 or signing an N11, you lose your rights to anything left in the unit after the termination date, and the landlord can keep, sell or throw it away. Take everything with you and don't plan to come back for items later.

**Do I pay rent for my last month if I paid last month's rent?**
No. A rent deposit must be applied to your last rent period, so if you gave proper notice you don't pay again for that month. Your landlord also owes any interest on the deposit. If the deposit plus interest is less than the final month's rent, you pay the difference.

## Sources

- [LTB Brochure: How a Tenant Can End Their Tenancy](https://tribunalsontario.ca/documents/ltb/Brochures/How%20a%20Tenant%20Can%20End%20Their%20Tenancy%20(EN).html)
- [Form N9: Tenant's Notice to End the Tenancy (LTB)](https://tribunalsontario.ca/documents/ltb/Notices%20of%20Termination%20&%20Instructions/N9.pdf)
- [Form N11: Agreement to End the Tenancy (LTB)](https://tribunalsontario.ca/documents/ltb/Other%20Forms/N11.pdf)
- [LTB Operational Update: Legislative Changes Effective September 21, 2026](https://tribunalsontario.ca/2026/09/21/ltb-operational-update-legislative-changes-at-the-landlord-and-tenant-board-effective-september-21-2026/)
- [Get your deposit back (Steps to Justice)](https://stepstojustice.ca/steps/housing-law/2-get-your-deposit-back/)
- [Can I come back for some of my things after moving day? (Steps to Justice)](https://stepstojustice.ca/questions/housing-law/can-i-come-back-some-my-things-after-moving-day/)
- [Change my address (Government of Ontario)](https://www.ontario.ca/page/change-my-address-ontario-services)
- [LTB Brochure: Information for New Tenants](https://tribunalsontario.ca/documents/ltb/Brochures/Information%20for%20New%20Tenants.html)
