# N12 and N13 Evictions in Ontario: 2026 Rules for Tenants

URL: https://www.colivease.ca/blog/n12-n13-eviction-ontario/
Language: English
Updated: 2026-11-03

N12 and N13 notices in Ontario: notice periods, compensation, the new 120-day N12 rule, your right to move back after renovations, and T5 bad-faith claims.

An **N12** is a landlord's notice to end your tenancy because the landlord, a buyer, or a close family member or caregiver will move in. An **N13** is for demolition, conversion to non-residential use, or renovations so big they need a building permit and an empty unit. Neither is an eviction order: you can stay until the Landlord and Tenant Board (LTB) decides, you're usually owed compensation, and if the landlord acted in bad faith, you can claim with a Form T5.

The rules shifted on September 21, 2026, so older articles may be out of date. Here's how both notices work now.

## Key takeaways

- **N12 notice:** at least 60 days, ending on the last day of a rental period or fixed term.
- **N13 notice:** at least 120 days, same end-of-period rule.
- **N12 compensation:** one month's rent or another acceptable unit, unless an own-use notice served on or after September 21, 2026 gives at least 120 days.
- **N13 compensation:** one or three months' rent depending on building size, adjusted if you plan to move back.
- **You don't have to leave** because of the notice alone. You can leave early with 10 days' notice on Form N9.
- **Bad faith?** File a T5. For own-use N12s, bad faith is now presumed if nobody moves in within 60 days.

*This article is general information, not legal advice. For your situation, contact the [Landlord and Tenant Board](https://tribunalsontario.ca/ltb/) or a community legal clinic (Legal Aid Ontario can refer you to one at 1-800-668-8258).*

## What changed on September 21, 2026

Amendments from Bill 60 and Bill 97 changed several no-fault eviction rules:

| Rule | Now |
|---|---|
| Own-use N12 compensation | Not required if the notice gives **120+ days** and ends at the end of a period or term (notices served on or after September 21, 2026) |
| Own-use N12 move-in | Bad faith presumed if the named person doesn't move in **within 60 days** |
| N13 right of first refusal | Landlord must give written completion dates and **at least 60 days** to move back |
| T5 for refusing your return | Deadline is the **later** of two years after you move out or six months after the work is done |
| Delaying an eviction | For N12 and N13 cases, the LTB can delay an eviction if it wouldn't be unfair to the landlord or other tenants |

Old versions of the N12, N13 and T5 forms are no longer accepted as of November 30, 2026.

## N12: landlord's or purchaser's own use

### Who can move in

An N12 can only be served for:

- the landlord
- the landlord's spouse
- a child or parent of the landlord or the landlord's spouse
- a caregiver for one of those people, if the person receiving care lives or will live in the building

Siblings, grandchildren, cousins, aunts and uncles don't qualify. Only **individual** landlords can use an own-use N12; a corporation can't.

The person must genuinely intend to live there for **at least one year**. Part-time use, an office, or leaving the unit empty doesn't count. The landlord must also file a sworn affidavit or declaration from the person who will move in.

### Sale to a buyer

A landlord who has signed an agreement of purchase and sale can serve an N12 for the **buyer's** use (or the buyer's spouse, child, parent or caregiver), but only if the building has **three or fewer units**, or the unit is a condo.

### Notice period

The termination date must be at least **60 days** after you get the notice and must fall on the last day of a rental period or fixed term. For example, if you pay monthly on the 1st and get the notice on January 20, the earliest valid date is March 31. A notice with the wrong date is defective and can't be fixed later.

### Compensation

| N12 type | What the landlord owes |
|---|---|
| Own use, under 120 days' notice | One month's rent or another acceptable unit, by the termination date |
| Own use, served on or after Sept 21, 2026 with 120+ days' notice | Nothing required |
| Purchaser's use (any notice length) | One month's rent or another acceptable unit, paid by the landlord who served it |

The LTB can't evict you on an N12 or N13 until any required compensation is paid. Compensation can also be a clearly stated rent waiver for a specific month, given before the termination date.

## N13: demolition, conversion or major renovations

A landlord can serve an N13 to demolish the unit, convert it to a non-residential use, or do repairs or renovations so extensive that they need a **building permit** and **vacant possession**. Work that doesn't need a permit, or that can be done while you live there, doesn't qualify. The LTB has also found that turning a unit into an Airbnb isn't a conversion to non-residential use.

At the hearing, the landlord must show they have the permits, or have taken all reasonable steps and the permits can't be issued until you leave.

### Notice period

At least **120 days**, ending on the last day of a rental period or fixed term.

### Toronto's renovation licence

In Toronto, the Rental Renovation Licence Bylaw requires landlords to get a City licence before renovations that need tenants to leave under the N13 process. Licence conditions include notifying tenants and arranging temporary accommodation or monthly rent-gap payments for tenants who are returning, or compensation for tenants who aren't. The LTB treats a required municipal licence as an approval the landlord must have before an eviction order. If you get an N13 in Toronto, use the City's Renovation Rights Assessment Tool or call the Federation of Metro Tenants' Associations hotline at 416-921-9494.

### Compensation

No compensation is owed if the landlord was **ordered** to do the work or demolish. Otherwise:

| Situation | 5 or more units | Fewer than 5 units |
|---|---|---|
| Demolition or conversion | 3 months' rent or another acceptable unit | 1 month's rent or another acceptable unit |
| Renovation, you're **not** returning | 3 months' rent or another acceptable unit | 1 month's rent or another acceptable unit |
| Renovation, you **are** returning | Rent for the lesser of 3 months or the renovation period | Rent for the lesser of 1 month or the renovation period |

### Your right to move back

After a renovation N13 (not demolition), you have a **right of first refusal**:

1. **Before you move out,** tell the landlord in writing that you want to return.
2. **Keep the landlord updated in writing** whenever your address changes.
3. Your rent on return can be no more than the landlord could have charged without the interruption.

If you gave written notice on or after September 21, 2026, the landlord must tell you in writing, without delay, the estimated completion date, any change to it, and when the unit is ready. For units ready on or after that date, you get **at least 60 days** to move back in.

## When you get an N12 or N13: what to do

1. **Check the notice.** Right form, right person (N12), right reason, right termination date.
2. **Note the deadlines.** The landlord must file an L2 application no later than 30 days after the termination date, or it's dismissed.
3. **Decide whether to stay or go.** If you want to leave sooner, give 10 days' written notice on an [N9](/blog/ending-a-tenancy-n9/).
4. **Make sure you're paid.** Compensation is due by the termination date. If it never comes, claim it with a T1 or as part of a T5.
5. **For an N13, send your right-of-first-refusal letter** before moving if you might want to return.
6. **Keep paying rent** while you stay.
7. **Go to the hearing** if one is scheduled. The LTB must consider whether to refuse or delay the eviction based on all the circumstances.

If the LTB later dismisses the landlord's application after you've been paid, you may have to give the compensation back.

## Bad-faith evictions and the T5 application

A **Form T5** is how a former tenant asks the LTB to rule that an N12 or N13 was given in bad faith.

### When it applies

- You moved out because of the notice, or an application or order based on it, **and**
- the named person didn't move in, or the work didn't happen, within a reasonable time.

### Presumptions that help tenants

For an own-use N12, bad faith is **presumed** (the landlord can try to prove otherwise) if:

- the named person didn't move in within **60 days** of the termination date, or of your move-out if you left later, for T5s filed after September 21, 2026; or
- between your notice and one year after you moved out, the landlord advertised the unit for rent or sale, rented it to someone else, demolished it, or took steps to convert it.

### Deadlines and fee

| T5 type | Deadline |
|---|---|
| Bad-faith N12 or N13 | One year after you moved out |
| Landlord refused your right to move back | Later of two years after you moved out or six months after the work was done |

The fee is $53, or $48 on the Tribunals Ontario Portal.

### What the LTB can order

- The extra rent you pay at your new place, for up to one year
- Reasonable moving, storage and similar costs
- General compensation of up to 12 months of your last rent, even without receipts
- A rent abatement
- An administrative fine
- In some cases, an order letting you move back in

Giving a notice in bad faith to get possession is also an **offence**. Maximum fines are $100,000 for individuals and $500,000 for corporations.

Gather evidence early: listing screenshots, mail addressed to the unit, photos, and what neighbours saw. Our guide to [LTB tenant applications](/blog/ltb-tenant-applications/) explains how to file and prepare.

## If you rent with roommates

If you're all on one lease, the notice and any eviction application should name every tenant on it, and the compensation is one month's (or three months') rent for the unit, not per person. Agree early on how you'll split it and whether you'll move together. If you rent a room from the owner and share their kitchen or bathroom, the RTA usually doesn't apply at all; see [living with your landlord in Ontario](/blog/living-with-your-landlord-ontario/).

## Bottom line

An N12 or N13 starts a process; it doesn't end your tenancy on its own. Check the dates, make sure compensation arrives on time, send your right-of-first-refusal letter for renovations, and keep an eye on the unit after you leave. The 2026 presumptions make bad-faith claims easier to prove.

## FAQ

**Do I have to move out when I get an N12 or N13?**
No. An N12 or N13 is only a notice. If you stay, your landlord must apply to the Landlord and Tenant Board and prove their case at a hearing, and only an LTB eviction order enforced by the Sheriff can remove you. You can also choose to leave earlier by giving 10 days' written notice on Form N9.

**Does my landlord still have to pay me one month's rent for an N12?**
Usually yes, by the termination date. The exception: for a landlord's own-use N12 served on or after September 21, 2026, no compensation or alternative unit is owed if the notice gives at least 120 days and ends on the last day of a rental period or fixed term. Purchaser N12s always require one month's rent.

**How much compensation do I get for an N13 renovation eviction?**
It depends on building size and whether you plan to return. In a building with five or more units, it's three months' rent, or another acceptable unit. With fewer than five units, it's one month. If you've told the landlord in writing you'll move back, it's the lesser of that amount and the rent for the time the work actually takes.

**What happens if my landlord doesn't move in after an N12?**
You can file a Form T5 within one year of moving out. Since September 21, 2026, bad faith is presumed if the person named on the notice doesn't move in within 60 days of the termination date or your move-out. The LTB can award rent differences for a year, moving costs and up to 12 months' rent as general compensation.

**Can I move back in after renovations under an N13?**
Yes, if you tell the landlord in writing before you move out and keep them updated on your address. Your rent must be no more than what the landlord could have charged without the interruption. The landlord must keep you informed of completion dates and give you at least 60 days to move back once the unit is ready.

## Sources

- [LTB Operational Update: Legislative changes effective September 21, 2026](https://tribunalsontario.ca/2026/09/21/ltb-operational-update-legislative-changes-at-the-landlord-and-tenant-board-effective-september-21-2026/)
- [LTB Interpretation Guideline 12: Eviction for Personal Use, Demolition, Repairs and Conversion](https://tribunalsontario.ca/documents/ltb/Interpretation%20Guidelines/12%20-%20Eviction%20for%20Personal%20Use.html)
- [Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (Ontario e-Laws)](https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/06r17)
- [Government of Ontario: Renting in Ontario, your rights](https://www.ontario.ca/page/renting-ontario-your-rights)
- [City of Toronto: Rental Renovation Licence Bylaw](https://www.toronto.ca/services-payments/permits-licences-bylaws/renovictions-bylaw-development/)
- [LTB: Forms, filing and fees](https://tribunalsontario.ca/ltb/forms-filing-and-fees/)

# Paying Rent in Ontario: Receipts, Cheques and Late Rent

URL: https://www.colivease.ca/blog/paying-rent-ontario/
Language: English
Updated: 2026-11-03

Paying rent in Ontario: due dates, free rent receipts, post-dated cheques and auto-pay rules, e-transfers, late rent and the 7-day N4, and deposit interest.

In Ontario, rent is due in full on the date set in your lease. Your landlord must give you a **free receipt** whenever you ask, and can't **require** post-dated cheques or automatic payments. Late fees aren't allowed, but if rent is even a day late a landlord can serve an **N4** notice, which now gives you **7 days** to pay before they can apply to the Landlord and Tenant Board (LTB).

Here's how each rule works, plus how to pay safely by e-transfer and what happens to the interest on your last month's rent.

## Key takeaways

- **Due date:** whatever your lease says. There's no legal grace period.
- **Receipts:** free on request, for rent, deposits and other charges, and for up to 12 months after you move out.
- **Post-dated cheques and auto-pay:** optional. A landlord can't refuse to rent to you or evict you for declining.
- **No late fees or interest on arrears.** A bounced payment can cost the bank's NSF fee plus up to $20.
- **N4 notice period:** 7 days for notices given on or after September 21, 2026.
- **Deposit interest:** 2.1% due in 2026, 1.9% due in 2027.

*This is general information, not legal advice. For your situation, contact the [Landlord and Tenant Board](https://tribunalsontario.ca/ltb/) or a community legal clinic through Legal Aid Ontario or Steps to Justice.*

## When rent is due

Your lease sets the due date and how rent is paid. On the Ontario Standard Lease, **section 5** lists the total rent, the day it's due, who to pay, the payment methods and any administration charge for cheques returned by a bank.

A few things to know:

- **Pay the full amount on time.** If the full rent isn't paid on the day it's due, the landlord can serve an N4. Partial payments still leave you in arrears.
- **Build in a buffer.** If the due date falls on a weekend or holiday, send your payment a few days early so it clearly arrives on time.
- **Roommates on one lease** are each responsible for the full rent, not just their share. If one person doesn't pay, the landlord can look to all of you. Our guide to [splitting rent fairly](/blog/split-rent-fairly/) covers how to set this up between you.

## Rent receipts: free, on request

Under the Residential Tenancies Act (RTA), your landlord must give you a receipt for any rent payment, rent deposit or other charge if you ask. They **can't charge** for it. Former tenants can ask for one within **12 months** after the tenancy ends. Refusing to give a receipt is an offence that you can report to the province's Rental Housing Enforcement Unit.

Ask for receipts even if you pay electronically. A good receipt shows:

- the date and amount paid
- the rental period it covers (for example, "rent for December 2026")
- the rental unit address
- the landlord's name and signature (or email confirmation)

Keep them in one folder. They're your proof if there's ever a dispute about what you paid.

## Post-dated cheques and automatic payments

A landlord **can't require** you to pay by:

- post-dated cheques
- pre-authorized debit from your bank account
- automatic credit card charges, or any other automatic payment

They can suggest these methods, and you can agree if you want to. But a landlord can't refuse to rent to you, or try to evict you, because you said no. This is true even if a lease clause says otherwise.

**Once a method is agreed, it stays** unless you both agree to change it. If your landlord suddenly demands a new app or method, you don't have to switch. If you do agree to change, put it in writing or keep the text or email.

## Paying by e-transfer

E-transfer is the most common method in Toronto. To use it safely:

- **Confirm the recipient.** The name shown when you add the payee should match the landlord or property manager on your lease.
- **Use the message field.** Write the address and period, for example "Unit 3, 123 Example St: rent Dec 2026".
- **Save confirmations.** Screenshot or export each one; your bank may not keep history forever.
- **Never send money before you've signed a lease** with a verified landlord. Requests to e-transfer a deposit to hold a unit you haven't seen are a classic scam. See [Toronto rental scams](/blog/toronto-rental-scams/).
- **Ask for a receipt anyway.** An e-transfer record proves money moved; a receipt confirms what it was for.

If you pay cash, always get a receipt on the spot.

## Late rent: what landlords can and can't do

### No late fees or interest

Ontario landlords **can't** charge late fees or interest on unpaid rent, and lease terms requiring them are void. What a landlord **can** recover:

- the **NSF fee** their bank charged if your cheque bounced or payment failed
- an **administration charge of up to $20** for that returned payment
- the LTB filing fee, if they apply and the LTB orders you to pay it

Landlords **can** offer a discount for paying on time. If your lease has one, you'll owe the full, undiscounted rent if you're late.

### The N4 notice

If rent is late, the landlord can give you **Form N4: Notice to End your Tenancy Early for Non-payment of Rent**.

- For an N4 given **on or after September 21, 2026**, the termination date must be at least **7 days** after the notice is given (it used to be 14 days for monthly tenancies).
- **You can void it.** Pay all the arrears in the notice, plus any rent that has come due since, before the landlord files an application, and the notice is cancelled. Get a receipt.
- **You don't have to move out** because of an N4. The landlord can apply to the LTB (Form L1) starting the day after the termination date, and only an LTB order enforced by the Sheriff can evict you.

### If the landlord applies to the LTB

- You can pay what's owed (including the filing fee) before the order is issued, work out a payment plan using the LTB's mandatory **Payment Agreement Form**, or go to the hearing.
- **New in 2026:** for applications filed on or after September 21, 2026, if you want to raise other issues at the hearing, such as repairs, you must pay the landlord **at least half of the arrears claimed** at least seven days before the hearing, and give written notice of the issues. Pay the landlord directly and keep a receipt.
- **Persistent late payment** now has a definition: rent received more than seven days after the due date at least three times within six months. That matters because persistent late payment is one of the reasons a landlord can give for trying to end a tenancy.
- Unpaid rent can also be reported to a credit bureau, which can make future rentals harder.

If you're struggling, talk to your landlord early and in writing, and contact a legal clinic. Withholding rent because of repair problems is risky; the LTB has tenant applications for that. Our sibling guides on [getting repairs done](/blog/landlord-repairs-ontario/) and [LTB tenant applications](/blog/ltb-tenant-applications/) explain the safer route.

## Your last month's rent deposit and its interest

If you paid a rent deposit (usually called last month's rent), your landlord must:

- use it **only** for your last rent period, not for damage or cleaning
- pay you **interest every year** at the rent increase guideline rate in effect when the interest is due

| Interest due in | Rate |
|---|---|
| 2026 | 2.1% |
| 2027 | 1.9% |

**Example:** you've paid a $2,000 deposit. When a year's interest falls due in 2026, it's $2,000 × 2.1% = $42.

When rent goes up, the landlord can ask you to increase the deposit by the same amount, and often uses the interest to do it, so the deposit keeps matching one month's rent. If your rent doesn't go up, the interest should be paid to you or credited against rent. Not paying deposit interest is an offence under the RTA; you can ask in writing and, if needed, apply to the LTB with Form T1.

For the full picture, see [rent deposit rules in Ontario](/blog/rent-deposit-rules-ontario/).

## Rent payment checklist

- [ ] Lease section 5 shows the amount, due date and payment method
- [ ] You chose the method; nobody required cheques or auto-pay
- [ ] Every payment has a receipt or saved confirmation
- [ ] E-transfers go to the name on the lease, with a clear memo
- [ ] No late fees or interest have been charged
- [ ] Deposit interest has been paid or added each year
- [ ] Roommates know the full rent is a shared responsibility

## Bottom line

Pay on time, pay in a way you chose and keep proof of every payment. If you fall behind, know that an N4 now gives you just 7 days, that you can void it by paying everything owed, and that only the LTB can end your tenancy.

## FAQ

**Does my landlord have to give me a rent receipt in Ontario?**
Yes, if you ask. A landlord must give a free receipt for rent, a rent deposit or any other charge you pay. Former tenants can also ask for one within 12 months after the tenancy ends. Charging for a receipt or refusing to give one is an offence under the Residential Tenancies Act.

**Can my landlord make me give post-dated cheques?**
No. A landlord can suggest post-dated cheques or automatic payments such as pre-authorized debits or credit card charges, but can't require them, refuse to rent to you or evict you for saying no. Once you and the landlord agree on a payment method, it can only change if you both agree.

**Can a landlord charge a late fee for rent in Ontario?**
No. Landlords can't charge late fees or interest on unpaid rent. If a cheque bounces or a payment fails, you may have to cover the bank's NSF fee plus an administration charge of up to $20. Discounts for paying on time are allowed, so read any discount terms in your lease carefully.

**How long does an N4 give me to pay late rent?**
For an N4 given on or after September 21, 2026, the termination date must be at least 7 days after the notice is given. If you pay all the rent owing, plus any rent that has since come due, before the landlord files an eviction application, the notice is void and you don't have to move.

**Do I get interest on my last month's rent deposit?**
Yes. Your landlord must pay interest on the rent deposit every year at the rent increase guideline rate in effect when it's due: 2.1% for interest due in 2026 and 1.9% for 2027. The landlord can pay it to you or use it to top up the deposit after a rent increase.

## Sources

- [LTB Brochure: A Guide to the Residential Tenancies Act](https://tribunalsontario.ca/documents/ltb/Brochures/A%20Guide%20to%20the%20Residential%20Tenancies%20Act.html)
- [LTB Brochure: If a Tenant Does Not Pay Rent](https://tribunalsontario.ca/documents/ltb/Brochures/If%20a%20Tenant%20Does%20Not%20Pay%20Rent%20(EN).html)
- [LTB Operational Update: Legislative Changes Effective September 21, 2026](https://tribunalsontario.ca/2026/09/21/ltb-operational-update-legislative-changes-at-the-landlord-and-tenant-board-effective-september-21-2026/)
- [Rental housing offences (Government of Ontario)](https://www.ontario.ca/page/rental-housing-offences)
- [Residential rent increases (Government of Ontario)](https://www.ontario.ca/page/residential-rent-increases)

# Pets in Rentals Ontario: Are No-Pet Clauses Legal?

URL: https://www.colivease.ca/blog/pets-in-rentals-ontario/
Language: English
Updated: 2026-11-03

Pets in Ontario rentals: why no-pet lease clauses are void under RTA section 14, the condo, allergy, damage and danger exceptions, and tips for roommates.

In most Ontario rentals, a "no pets" clause in your lease is **void**. Section 14 of the Residential Tenancies Act (RTA) cancels any lease term that bans animals, even if you signed it. The exceptions are condo rules that prohibit pets, rentals where you share a kitchen or bathroom with the owner, and pets that cause real problems: the Landlord and Tenant Board (LTB) can end a tenancy over an animal that seriously disturbs others, triggers a serious allergic reaction, or is inherently dangerous.

Here's what that means in practice, what landlords can and can't do, and how to keep the peace when your roommate has a cat and you don't.

## Key takeaways

- **No-pet lease terms are void** under RTA section 14 in most private rentals.
- **Condo rules can still ban pets,** and tenants have to follow them.
- **Live-in owner arrangements** (shared kitchen or bathroom) usually fall outside the RTA, so a no-pet rule there can be enforced as part of your agreement.
- **Eviction over a pet** needs an LTB order and proof of substantial interference, a serious allergic reaction, or an inherently dangerous animal.
- **No pet deposits** or damage deposits. But you pay for damage your pet causes beyond normal wear and tear.
- **Service animals** are protected under the Human Rights Code.

*This article is general information, not legal advice. For your situation, contact the [Landlord and Tenant Board](https://tribunalsontario.ca/ltb/) or a community legal clinic (Legal Aid Ontario can refer you to one at 1-800-668-8258).*

## What section 14 actually says

Section 14 of the RTA voids any provision in a tenancy agreement that prohibits animals in or around the building. Ontario's guide to the standard lease uses the same example: an extra term that doesn't allow pets is void and can't be enforced. Steps to Justice puts it simply: you don't have to follow a no-pets rule even if it's written into your agreement.

"Void" means the clause has no legal effect. Your landlord can't evict you just for breaking it, and can't use it to charge you extra.

### What section 14 doesn't do

It protects terms in a **tenancy agreement**. It doesn't force a landlord to pick a pet owner when choosing between applicants. Plenty of Toronto landlords ask about pets, and having a pet isn't one of the protected grounds under Ontario's Human Rights Code. Be honest if asked; misrepresenting things on an application is a bad way to start a tenancy.

### Service and support animals

Disability is a protected ground. The Ontario Human Rights Commission says that accommodating people with disabilities can include changing "no pets" policies to allow guide dogs and other service animals, including animals that help with needs such as anxiety. The animal doesn't have to be certified, but where its role isn't obvious, you may need to show documentation, such as a letter from a doctor or other qualified health professional.

## The exceptions

### 1. Condo rules

If you rent a condo, the **Condominium Act** requires everyone who occupies a unit, tenants included, to follow the condo's declaration, bylaws and rules. Some condo declarations restrict or ban pets. Section 14 of the RTA doesn't override that.

The Ontario standard lease asks the landlord to note if the unit is a condo, and you agree to follow the condo rules the landlord gives you. **Ask for them before you sign.** If a condo pet ban applies and you bring an animal in anyway, your landlord could serve a notice saying you're substantially interfering with their lawful rights, which can lead to an eviction application.

### 2. Living with the owner

If you share a kitchen or bathroom with the owner who lives there, the RTA generally doesn't apply, so section 14 doesn't protect you. Whatever you agreed about pets is what counts. See our guide to [living with your landlord in Ontario](/blog/living-with-your-landlord-ontario/).

### 3. Problems caused by the animal

Section 76 of the RTA says the LTB can't end a tenancy over an animal unless it's satisfied you keep the animal and that:

| Ground | What the landlord must show |
|---|---|
| Disturbance | The past behaviour of an animal of that species **substantially interfered** with the reasonable enjoyment of the building by the landlord or other tenants |
| Allergy | The presence of an animal of that species caused the landlord or another tenant a **serious allergic reaction** |
| Danger | The species or breed is **inherently dangerous** to the safety of the landlord or other tenants |

The Board won't evict on the disturbance or allergy grounds if your own animal **didn't cause or contribute** to the problem.

### 4. Damage

If you, someone living with you or a guest wilfully or negligently causes undue damage (for example, by letting a pet wreck the floors), the landlord can serve a notice under section 62 of the RTA. You get **seven days** to repair it, pay for it, or make arrangements the landlord accepts, and if you do, the notice is void.

## How a pet-related eviction actually works

A landlord can't just tell you the dog has to go. For behaviour like constant barking or an aggressive animal, the usual route is an **N5** notice for substantial interference:

1. The notice must give a termination date at least **20 days** away, explain the problem, and ask you to fix it **within seven days**.
2. If you fix the problem within those seven days, the first notice is void.
3. If you don't, the landlord can apply to the LTB, and you get a hearing.
4. Only an LTB order, enforced by the Sheriff, can remove you.

## What landlords can and can't do

**Landlords can:**

- ask about pets when screening new applicants
- require you to follow condo rules that restrict pets
- serve proper notices and apply to the LTB if an animal causes real problems
- make you pay for damage beyond normal wear and tear
- enter with 24 hours' written notice for repairs and inspections, and you must secure your pet so the work can happen

**Landlords can't:**

- enforce a no-pet clause in a regular RTA tenancy
- charge a pet deposit, pet damage deposit or other deposit beyond a rent deposit and a refundable key deposit (see our guide to [deposit rules in Ontario](/blog/rent-deposit-rules-ontario/))
- evict you without an LTB order
- enter without proper notice to "check on the pet" (our guide to [landlord entry rules](/blog/landlord-entry-rules-ontario/) explains the rules)

## Tips for renters with pets

- **Be upfront** with landlords you're applying to. A short pet profile with age, vaccination records, spay or neuter status and a past landlord reference helps.
- **Ask for condo rules** in writing if the unit is in a condo.
- **Document the unit at move-in** with dated photos and video, especially floors, doors and screens.
- **Deal with complaints quickly.** If a neighbour mentions barking, respond before it becomes a notice.
- **Look into tenant insurance** and whether it covers liability for your pet; our guide to [tenant insurance in Ontario](/blog/tenant-insurance-ontario/) covers what to ask.

## Pets and roommates

Section 14 is about you and your landlord. It doesn't settle anything between roommates, and the LTB doesn't hear roommate disputes. Talk it through before anyone signs:

- **Allergies:** a serious allergy in the household is a dealbreaker conversation, not a "we'll see".
- **Who's responsible:** feeding, walks, litter, vet bills and cleaning up shared spaces.
- **Damage:** who pays if the cat shreds the couch or the dog scratches the door.
- **Quiet and guests:** crate times, barking, and pets meeting visitors.
- **Exit plan:** what happens to the pet if the owner moves out.

Write it into a [roommate agreement](/blog/roommate-agreement-ontario/) so there's no confusion later.

## Bottom line

In most Ontario rentals, your landlord can't hold you to a no-pets clause. Condo rules, live-in owner arrangements and genuinely problematic animals are the exceptions, and you're always on the hook for damage. Keep your pet's record clean, read the condo rules, and agree on pet terms with roommates before moving in.

## FAQ

**Is a no-pets clause in my Ontario lease enforceable?**
Generally no. Section 14 of the Residential Tenancies Act makes any lease term that bans animals in the unit or building void, even if you signed it. The main exceptions are condo rules that prohibit certain pets, and rentals where you share a kitchen or bathroom with the owner, because the Act usually doesn't apply there.

**Can my landlord evict me because I have a pet?**
Only through the Landlord and Tenant Board, and only for specific reasons. The Board must be satisfied that the animal substantially interfered with others' reasonable enjoyment, caused the landlord or another tenant a serious allergic reaction, or is a species or breed that's inherently dangerous. It won't evict if your animal didn't cause or contribute to the problem.

**Can a landlord charge a pet deposit in Ontario?**
No. The Ontario government's guide to the standard lease lists damage and pet deposits as charges a lease can't require. A landlord can collect only a rent deposit of up to one month's rent and a refundable key deposit. If your pet causes damage beyond normal wear and tear, though, you're responsible for repairing it or paying for it.

**Can a landlord refuse to rent to me because I have a pet?**
The no-pet rule in section 14 protects you once you have a tenancy agreement. When choosing tenants, many landlords still ask about pets, and having a pet isn't a protected ground under the Human Rights Code. A disability-related service animal is different: landlords may have a duty to accommodate it, even with a no-pets policy.

**Do condo no-pet rules apply to tenants?**
Yes. Under the Condominium Act, occupiers, including tenants, must follow the condo's declaration, bylaws and rules. If the unit is a condo, the standard lease says you agree to follow the rules the landlord gives you. Ask for the condo's pet rules before you sign, because they can prohibit some or all animals.

## Sources

- [Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, sections 14, 62, 64 and 76 (Ontario e-Laws)](https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/06r17)
- [Government of Ontario: Guide to Ontario's standard lease](https://www.ontario.ca/page/guide-ontarios-standard-lease)
- [Government of Ontario: Renting in Ontario, your rights](https://www.ontario.ca/page/renting-ontario-your-rights)
- [Condominium Act, 1998 (Ontario e-Laws)](https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/98c19)
- [Ontario Human Rights Commission: Policy on ableism and discrimination based on disability, duty to accommodate](https://www.ohrc.on.ca/en/policy-ableism-and-discrimination-based-disability/8-duty-accommodate)
- [LTB Interpretation Guideline 19: The Landlord's Right of Entry](https://tribunalsontario.ca/documents/ltb/Interpretation%20Guidelines/19%20-%20The%20Landlords%20Right%20of%20Entry%20into%20a%20Rental%20Unit.html)
- [Steps to Justice: What should be in my rental agreement?](https://stepstojustice.ca/questions/housing-law/what-should-be-my-rental-agreement/)

# Rental Viewing Checklist Toronto: What to Check and Ask

URL: https://www.colivease.ca/blog/rental-viewing-checklist-toronto/
Language: English
Updated: 2026-11-03

Rental viewing checklist for Toronto: test water, heat and alarms, check for pests and noise, ask the right questions, spot scams and compare places afterwards.

A good Toronto rental viewing takes 20 to 30 minutes and follows a plan: test the water, heat and windows, look for pests, damp and safety alarms, check laundry, noise and phone signal, then ask the landlord about rent, deposits, utilities and repairs. Leave with photos and notes, and never pay a deposit until you've verified the landlord and seen a lease.

Print this checklist or keep it open on your phone at your next viewing.

## Key takeaways

- **Test, don't just look.** Run taps, flush the toilet, open windows, check your phone signal.
- **Know the city minimums:** 21°C from October 1 to May 15 when the landlord supplies heat, and hot water between 45°C and 49°C at the taps.
- **Find the alarms.** Every Ontario home needs working smoke alarms on every storey and outside sleeping areas, plus CO alarms where there's a fuel-burning appliance or attached garage.
- **Ask who lives there.** If you'd share a kitchen or bathroom with the owner, the Residential Tenancies Act (RTA) usually doesn't apply.
- **Pay nothing at the viewing.** No cash, wires or crypto, and no "holding fee".

*This is general information, not legal advice. For your situation, contact the [Landlord and Tenant Board](https://tribunalsontario.ca/ltb/) or a community legal clinic through Legal Aid Ontario or Steps to Justice.*

## Before you go

- Look up the address on a map and walk or transit the route at the time you'd normally commute.
- Search the address and a few phrases from the listing to see if the same photos appear elsewhere at a different price.
- For apartment buildings with three or more storeys and ten or more units, check the building's **RentSafeTO** evaluation on the City's interactive map. Buildings get a green, yellow or red sign based on their score.
- Bring your phone (camera, flashlight, a timer), a small notebook and this list.
- If you're viewing as a group, decide in advance who checks what, so nothing gets missed while everyone looks at the kitchen.

## What to inspect

### Water pressure and hot water

- Turn on the kitchen tap and shower at the same time, then flush the toilet. Does the pressure collapse?
- Time how long hot water takes to arrive. Toronto requires hot water at the fixtures to be between 45°C and 49°C.
- Look under sinks for leaks, warped cabinet floors or water stains.

### Heat and cooling

- Ask how the unit is heated (radiators, baseboards, forced air) and who controls the thermostat.
- When heat is supplied at the landlord's expense, the City requires a minimum of **21°C from October 1 to May 15**.
- If the landlord provides air conditioning, it must be run from June 1 to September 30 to keep the unit at no more than 26°C. Landlords don't have to install AC where there isn't any.
- Check whether heat is included in rent or billed to you. Ask for last winter's bills if it isn't.

### Pests, damp and mould

- Use your flashlight under the sink, behind the stove and along baseboards for droppings, dead insects or traps.
- Check mattress seams and furniture joints in furnished rooms for small dark spots, a common sign of bed bugs.
- Ask directly: "Has the unit or building been treated for pests in the past year?"
- In basements, sniff for a musty smell and look for peeling paint, efflorescence (white powder) on walls and condensation on windows.

### Windows, doors and locks

- Open, close and lock every window. Look for drafts, broken screens and fogging between panes.
- Check bedroom windows in basements: are they big enough to climb out of? Our post on [legal basement apartments in Toronto](/blog/legal-basement-apartments-toronto/) explains why this matters.
- Test the front door lock and ask who else has keys.

### Smoke and carbon monoxide alarms

- Ontario law requires working smoke alarms on **every storey and outside all sleeping areas**, in rented homes as well as owned ones.
- A **CO alarm** is required near sleeping areas if the unit has a fuel-burning appliance or fireplace, or sits beside, above or below a garage or service room. In rental units, the landlord is responsible for installing and maintaining CO alarms.
- Press the test button only with the landlord's okay, but at least confirm the alarms are there and not disconnected.

### Electrical, kitchen and bathroom

- Count the outlets in each room and check that they work (bring a phone charger).
- Open the fridge, turn on a stove element and run the bathroom fan.
- Look at the caulking around the tub and the grout for mould.

### Laundry

- In-suite, shared in the building or none? If shared: how many machines, what hours, coins or a card?
- If there's no laundry, find the nearest laundromat now, not after you move in.

### Noise and neighbours

- Stand quietly for a minute with the windows closed, then open. Listen for streetcars, traffic, bars and HVAC units.
- Ask about the people upstairs and next door. In a house, ask how many units share it.
- If you can, walk past again on a Friday night.

### Cell signal and internet

- Check your bars in every room, especially basements and interior bedrooms, and make a short call.
- Ask which internet providers serve the building and whether internet is included.

## What to ask the landlord

| Topic | Questions to ask |
|---|---|
| Who's who | What's your full legal name and the address for notices? Are you the owner or an agent? |
| Who lives here | Will I share a kitchen or bathroom with the owner or the owner's family? |
| Rent | What's the total monthly rent? What's included (heat, hydro, water, internet, parking)? |
| Deposits | Is there a last month's rent deposit or a key deposit? Any other fees? |
| Rent increases | Was the unit first occupied as a residence after November 15, 2018? (If so, it may be exempt from the rent increase guideline.) |
| Repairs | How do I request repairs, and who handles emergencies after hours? |
| Rules | Are there condo rules or house rules I'll be asked to follow? |
| Timing | When can I move in, and when do you need an answer? |

On deposits, Ontario allows only a rent deposit of up to one month's rent and a refundable key deposit. Damage, pet and cleaning deposits aren't permitted. Our guide to [rent deposit rules in Ontario](/blog/rent-deposit-rules-ontario/) has the details.

## Documents to request

- **A draft of the Ontario Standard Lease.** It's required for most private residential tenancies signed on or after April 30, 2018. The landlord must give you a copy of the signed lease within 21 days. See our [guide to Ontario's standard lease](/blog/ontario-standard-lease/).
- **Proof of who you're dealing with.** Photo ID that matches the name on the lease, and if an agent shows the unit, something showing they're authorized to act for the owner.
- **Condo declaration, bylaws and rules** if the unit is in a condo. You'll be agreeing to follow them.
- **House rules or a roommate agreement** if you're joining an existing household.
- **The RentSafeTO evaluation**, for buildings in the program. Owners must share the score and details with prospective tenants.

Most landlords will also ask you for documents. Our [rental application guide](/blog/rental-application-toronto/) covers what's reasonable to share.

## Scam signs at or before a viewing

Canada's Competition Bureau flags these patterns, and they show up in Toronto every moving season:

- The rent is noticeably lower than similar places nearby.
- The "landlord" is abroad and can't show you inside, or offers only exterior photos.
- You're asked for a deposit before any lease exists, or to send money outside the country.
- Photos don't match the address, or appear on other listings.
- You're pushed to decide fast because "others are interested".
- A link sends you to a site asking for banking or personal details.

If something feels off, walk away. Our full guide to [Toronto rental scams](/blog/toronto-rental-scams/) covers how to verify a landlord and where to report fraud.

## How to compare places afterwards

Score each place the same evening, while it's fresh:

| Factor | Place A | Place B | Place C |
|---|---|---|---|
| Total monthly cost (rent + utilities) | | | |
| Commute time | | | |
| Water, heat, windows (1–5) | | | |
| Pests, damp, mould (1–5) | | | |
| Noise and signal (1–5) | | | |
| Laundry and storage (1–5) | | | |
| Landlord answers and documents (1–5) | | | |
| Gut feeling (1–5) | | | |

Compare **total** cost, not rent alone: a cheaper unit with hydro and heat billed separately can end up costing more. If you're applying with roommates, share the scores and agree on a first choice before anyone submits an application.

## Bottom line

A viewing is your one chance to find problems before they become yours. Test the basics, ask direct questions, collect documents and pay nothing until the landlord and lease check out. Then compare places on the same scorecard.

## FAQ

**What should I check when viewing an apartment in Toronto?**
Run the taps and shower together to test water pressure and hot water, look for signs of pests and mould, open and lock every window, find the smoke and carbon monoxide alarms, check the laundry setup, listen for noise and test your phone signal in each room. Take photos so you can compare places later.

**How warm does a landlord have to keep a Toronto rental?**
If the landlord provides heat, City of Toronto rules require a minimum of 21°C from October 1 to May 15. Hot water at the taps must be between 45°C and 49°C. If a heat problem isn't fixed within 24 hours of telling your landlord, you can call 311 so the City can investigate.

**Should I pay a deposit at a viewing?**
No. Don't pay anything until you've seen the inside of the unit, confirmed who the landlord is and reviewed a lease. In Ontario, a landlord can only collect a rent deposit of up to one month's rent and a refundable key deposit. Requests for cash or a wire transfer on the spot are common scam signs.

**What documents should I ask for before renting?**
Ask for a draft of the Ontario Standard Lease, the landlord's full name and address for notices, proof that the person showing the unit is the owner or authorized to act for them, any condo rules or house rules, and, for larger apartment buildings, the RentSafeTO evaluation score the owner must share with prospective tenants.

**Does the Residential Tenancies Act apply if I share a kitchen with the owner?**
Usually not. Ontario's Residential Tenancies Act generally doesn't apply if you must share a kitchen or bathroom with the owner or certain close family members of the owner who live there. Ask about this at the viewing, because it affects deposits, notice and eviction protections.

## Sources

- [Indoor Temperatures in Apartment Units (City of Toronto)](https://www.toronto.ca/community-people/housing-shelter/rental-housing-rights-information/housing-property-standards/indoor-temperatures-in-apartment-units/)
- [Heat & Other Vital Services in Rental Units (City of Toronto)](https://www.toronto.ca/city-government/public-notices-bylaws/bylaw-enforcement/not-enough-heatother-vital-services/)
- [RentSafeTO: Evaluations & Audits (City of Toronto)](https://www.toronto.ca/community-people/housing-shelter/rental-housing-rights-information/housing-property-standards/apartment-building-standards/audits-evaluations/)
- [Carbon monoxide safety (Government of Ontario)](https://www.ontario.ca/page/carbon-monoxide-safety)
- [Fire safety at home (Government of Ontario)](https://www.ontario.ca/page/fire-safety-home)
- [LTB Brochure: Information for New Tenants](https://tribunalsontario.ca/documents/ltb/Brochures/Information%20for%20New%20Tenants.html)

# Roommate Guest Rules: Partners, Overnights and Rent

URL: https://www.colivease.ca/blog/roommate-guest-rules/
Language: English
Updated: 2026-11-03

Fair roommate guest rules for Toronto: overnight limits, a partner who's basically living there, rent and bills, occupant vs tenant, and template wording.

Fair roommate guest rules set a clear overnight limit (many households use two to four nights a week per person), require a heads-up for longer stays, and say when a regular guest starts paying toward bills. In Ontario, a landlord generally can't ban guests, but a partner who moves in doesn't become a tenant just by living there, so the people on the lease stay responsible for the rent.

Guests are one of the most common sources of roommate tension. Here's how to set rules everyone can live with, handle the partner who's "basically living here", and keep the lease side straight.

## Key takeaways

- **Agree on numbers**, not vibes: nights per week, notice, and quiet hours.
- **Landlords generally can't ban guests** in tenancies covered by the Residential Tenancies Act (RTA).
- **An occupant isn't a tenant.** A partner who moves in without the landlord's agreement usually has no lease rights and no lease obligations.
- **Set a trigger for contributing**, such as more than 10 nights a month.
- **Write it into your roommate agreement** so the rule exists before the conflict does.

## What your landlord can and can't do about guests

Ontario's guide to the standard lease lists terms that "do not allow guests, roommates, any additional occupants" as examples of void terms that can't be enforced in RTA tenancies. The government's renting guide also says plainly that landlords can't ban guests.

That doesn't mean anything goes:

- **Damage.** Tenants must repair or pay for undue damage caused by them or their guests.
- **Behaviour.** The LTB's guide to the Act explains that a landlord can give a tenant notice over problems caused by the tenant's guest or someone else living in the unit, so a guest's conduct can put your tenancy at risk.
- **Overcrowding.** The LTB's N5 notice covers interfering with others, damage and overcrowding, so a landlord can act if the number of people living in a unit becomes a genuine problem.
- **Condo rules.** In a condo, building rules (for example, on amenity bookings or move-ins) still apply.
- **Living with the owner.** If you share a kitchen or bathroom with the owner or their close family, the RTA generally doesn't apply, and the owner's house rules on guests can be much stricter. Read your agreement.

The bigger question for most people isn't the landlord. It's the other roommates.

## Fair house rules for guests

There's no legal standard for roommate guest rules, so the right answer is whatever your household agrees. These defaults work for a lot of shared homes:

| Topic | A fair starting point |
|---|---|
| Daytime guests | Fine anytime; mention it if you'll use the living room for a group |
| Overnight guests | Up to 3 nights a week per roommate, with a heads-up by text |
| Longer stays | Ask everyone first for anything over 3 nights in a row |
| Parties | Agree a date at least a few days ahead; end by an agreed time |
| Quiet hours | Same rules for guests as for roommates |
| Bathroom | Guests don't shower in peak morning slots on workdays |
| Keys and codes | No copies or door codes for guests without everyone's agreement |
| Food | Guests don't eat shared groceries unless the host replaces them |
| Responsibility | The host cleans up after their guest and covers any damage |

Adjust for your home. A two-bedroom with one bathroom needs tighter rules than a large house with three bathrooms.

## The partner who's "basically living here"

It usually happens gradually: a toothbrush, then a drawer, then five nights a week. Signs a guest has effectively moved in:

- They're there more nights than not
- They receive mail or packages at the address
- They have their own key
- Shared groceries, hot water and hydro use have noticeably risen
- Other roommates feel they can't use the common areas

### How to raise it

Talk to your roommate, not their partner, and keep it about the arrangement rather than the person: "Sam's here most nights now, which is fine with us, but our bills have gone up and the bathroom's busier in the morning. Can we talk about what's fair?"

Then pick one of three paths:

1. **Scale back** to the agreed overnight limit.
2. **Contribute.** The partner chips in toward utilities, internet and shared supplies, and possibly a share of rent, under your roommate agreement.
3. **Move in properly.** Everyone agrees, the landlord is told, and the lease is updated if the landlord agrees.

## Rent, utilities and the lease: occupant vs tenant

### Occupant

A partner who moves in without signing the lease or being accepted by the landlord is usually an **occupant**. In general:

- They aren't responsible to the landlord for rent or damage under the lease (the tenants are).
- They have few or no rights against the landlord, and usually can't bring a case to the LTB.
- If the tenant they live with leaves, they generally have no right to stay.

### Tenant

To become a **tenant**, the landlord normally has to agree, for example by adding the person to the lease. Ontario's standard lease requires the landlord's consent for an assignment or sublet, and says the landlord can't arbitrarily or unreasonably withhold it. See [sublet and assignment in Ontario](/blog/sublet-and-assignment-ontario/) for how that works.

### Can the landlord charge more?

In an RTA tenancy, rent increases follow set rules: generally at least 12 months apart, with 90 days' written notice on the proper LTB form, and, for most units, no more than the yearly guideline without LTB approval. The standard lease guide also says terms requiring fees or deposits the Act doesn't permit are void. If your landlord demands extra money because someone moved in, get advice from the LTB or a legal clinic before paying.

### Utilities

If utilities are in a roommate's name, a long-term guest adds real costs. A simple fix is to split variable bills (hydro, gas) by the number of people actually living there, and fixed ones (internet) by the roommates. Our guide to [utilities for Toronto renters](/blog/utilities-for-renters-toronto/) explains which bills you're likely to see, and [how to split rent fairly](/blog/split-rent-fairly/) covers rent shares.

## Template wording you can adapt

Add these clauses to your [roommate agreement](/blog/roommate-agreement-ontario/), changing the numbers to suit your home.

**Overnight guests:**

> Each roommate may have overnight guests up to three nights per week. Please give the others a heads-up by text the same day. Stays longer than three nights in a row need everyone's agreement in advance.

**Regular guests and costs:**

> If one roommate's guest stays more than 10 nights in a calendar month, we'll meet to review costs. Unless we agree otherwise, that roommate will pay an extra share of hydro, gas and shared supplies for that month, calculated as if the guest were an additional roommate.

**Moving a partner in:**

> No one moves in, including a partner, without the agreement of all roommates. If we agree, we'll tell the landlord, and we'll update this agreement with the new rent and bill shares from the move-in date.

**Responsibility:**

> The host is responsible for their guests' behaviour, cleaning up after them, and paying for any damage they cause.

**Keys and safety:**

> Guests don't get their own keys, fobs or door codes without everyone's agreement.

## If the rules aren't working

Revisit them at a house meeting rather than in the moment. If a guest situation turns into a bigger dispute about money or someone refusing to leave, our guide to [dealing with a bad roommate](/blog/dealing-with-a-bad-roommate/) covers mediation, Small Claims Court and when to get legal help. If anyone feels unsafe because of a guest, call 911 in an emergency.

## Start with people who share your expectations

## Bottom line

Pick clear numbers for overnight stays, agree when a regular guest starts paying, and write it down. Landlords generally can't ban guests in RTA tenancies, but a partner who moves in is usually an occupant, not a tenant, until the landlord agrees otherwise, so the people on the lease stay on the hook.

*This article is general information, not legal advice. For your specific situation, contact the Landlord and Tenant Board or a community legal clinic.*

## FAQ

**Can my landlord ban guests in Ontario?**
Generally no. Ontario's guide to the standard lease lists terms that don't allow guests, roommates or additional occupants as examples of void terms that can't be enforced in tenancies covered by the Residential Tenancies Act. Tenants are still responsible for undue damage their guests cause, and condo rules or overcrowding standards can still apply.

**How many nights a week can a guest stay over?**
There's no legal number for roommates; it's whatever your household agrees. Many groups settle on two to four nights a week per person, with a heads-up for anything longer. The key is to pick a number, write it down, and agree what happens when someone goes over it regularly, such as contributing to bills.

**Does my partner become a tenant if they move in?**
Not automatically. Someone who moves in without signing the lease or being accepted by the landlord is usually an occupant, not a tenant. They generally don't have a tenant's rights against the landlord, and they aren't responsible to the landlord for rent. To become a tenant, the landlord normally has to agree, for example by adding them to the lease.

**Should a partner who stays over a lot pay rent?**
Many households ask a regular overnight guest to chip in once they're there more than an agreed number of nights, often starting with utilities and shared groceries rather than rent. Whatever you choose, money should go to the roommates under your own agreement, and it doesn't change what the tenants owe the landlord under the lease.

**Can my landlord raise the rent because my partner moved in?**
In a tenancy covered by the RTA, rent increases follow set rules: generally at least 12 months apart, with 90 days' written notice on the proper form, and, for most units, within the yearly guideline unless the LTB approves more. Fees that the Act doesn't permit can't be added by the lease. If you're unsure, contact the LTB or a legal clinic.

## Sources

- [Guide to Ontario's standard lease (Government of Ontario)](https://www.ontario.ca/page/guide-ontarios-standard-lease)
- [Renting in Ontario: Your rights (Government of Ontario)](https://www.ontario.ca/page/renting-ontario-your-rights)
- [Residential rent increases (Government of Ontario)](https://www.ontario.ca/page/residential-rent-increases)
- [Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (Ontario e-Laws)](https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/06r17)
- [Forms, including the N5 notice (Landlord and Tenant Board)](https://tribunalsontario.ca/ltb/forms-filing-and-fees/)
- [Find out if the Residential Tenancies Act applies (Steps to Justice)](https://stepstojustice.ca/steps/housing-law/1-find-out-if-the-residential-tenancies-act-applies/)
- [A Guide to the Residential Tenancies Act (Landlord and Tenant Board)](https://tribunalsontario.ca/documents/ltb/Brochures/A%20Guide%20to%20the%20Residential%20Tenancies%20Act.html)

# Short-Term Rentals Toronto: Rules for Renters in 2026

URL: https://www.colivease.ca/blog/short-term-rentals-toronto/
Language: English
Updated: 2026-11-03

Short-term and furnished rentals in Toronto: the 28-night rule, principal residence and registration, when the RTA protects you, sublets and how to avoid scams.

In Toronto, a **short-term rental** is a stay of **less than 28 consecutive days**. It's only legal in the host's **principal residence** and must carry a City **registration number** (STR-0000-XXXXXX) in the listing. Longer furnished stays aren't short-term rentals under the bylaw, and whether Ontario's Residential Tenancies Act (RTA) protects you depends on whether the place is your home or temporary accommodation.

Here's what that means if you're the one looking for a furnished place, whether for a few weeks after landing or a few months during a work term.

## Key takeaways

- **Under 28 consecutive nights** = short-term rental under Toronto's bylaw.
- **Principal residence only.** Hosts can rent out the home they actually live in, not investment units.
- **Look for the registration number.** No number, no booking.
- **Entire homes** can be rented short-term for at most 180 nights a year.
- **The RTA generally doesn't cover** seasonal or temporary accommodation, or homes where you share a kitchen or bathroom with the owner.
- **Sublets are different:** a tenant leaves temporarily and plans to return, with the landlord's consent.

*This is general information, not legal advice. For your situation, contact the [Landlord and Tenant Board](https://tribunalsontario.ca/ltb/) or a community legal clinic through Legal Aid Ontario or Steps to Justice.*

## Toronto's short-term rental rules, in plain terms

The City's rules are aimed at hosts, but knowing them helps you spot a listing that shouldn't exist.

### The 28-night threshold

A short-term rental is all or part of a dwelling rented for **less than 28 consecutive days** in exchange for payment. That includes bed and breakfasts but excludes hotels, motels and student residences owned or run by publicly funded or non-profit schools. A stay of 28 consecutive days or more isn't a short-term rental under the bylaw.

### Principal residence

Short-term rentals are only allowed in the operator's **principal residence**: the home they live in and use for bills, ID, taxes and insurance. A person can only have one, so they can't legally run more than one short-term rental. Owners and renters can both qualify. In a duplex or triplex, the host can only short-term rent the unit they live in.

### Registration and limits

- Operators must **register with the City** and renew every year. The City-issued number must appear in the listing.
- Only **one registration per dwelling unit** is allowed.
- Hosts register either as **entire-unit** (the host isn't there during your stay) or **partial-unit** (the host lives there and rents rooms).
- An entire home can be rented for a maximum of **180 nights per calendar year**. Partial-unit hosts can rent up to three bedrooms for an unlimited number of nights, but can't rent out the whole unit at once.
- Platforms such as Airbnb and Booking.com must be **licensed** by the City.

### What a guest is entitled to

- A **24-hour contact** person during your stay.
- A posted **diagram of the building's exits**, physically displayed in the rental.
- **No discrimination** based on grounds such as race, citizenship, sex, gender identity, age, family status or disability, including refusing a guest with a service animal.

You can call **311** or submit a complaint online if a short-term rental is unregistered, isn't the host's principal residence, is unsafe or is a nuisance.

## When the RTA applies to longer furnished stays

Many newcomers, students and contract workers look for furnished places for one to six months. The key question is whether you're getting a **tenancy** covered by the RTA or **temporary accommodation** that isn't.

The RTA covers most rental housing in Ontario, including apartments, houses, basement units and rooms in rooming houses. It generally **doesn't** apply when:

- the accommodation is used on a **seasonal or temporary basis**, such as a hotel, cottage or vacation rental
- you **share a kitchen or bathroom with the owner** or the owner's close family members who live there

Furniture on its own isn't one of those exemptions. What matters is the nature of the arrangement. A furnished apartment you rent as your home for several months, with monthly rent, looks very different from a weekend platform booking.

**Why it matters:** if the RTA applies, you get protections like the Ontario Standard Lease, deposit limits (last month's rent and a refundable key deposit only), notice rules and the right to a hearing before any eviction. If it doesn't, your rights mostly come from your contract.

**Practical steps:**

- Ask the landlord directly: "Is this a tenancy under the Residential Tenancies Act?" and "Will I share a kitchen or bathroom with you?"
- Ask for the **Ontario Standard Lease**. It's required for most private residential tenancies.
- Read any "short-term" or "vacation" wording carefully. If a place you'll live in as your home is labelled temporary, get advice from the LTB or a legal clinic before you sign or pay.
- Our guide to [Ontario tenant rights](/blog/ontario-tenant-rights/) covers what you get when the RTA applies, and [living with your landlord](/blog/living-with-your-landlord-ontario/) explains the shared-kitchen exemption.

## Sublets versus short-term stays

These get mixed up in listings, but they're different arrangements.

| | Sublet | Short-term rental |
|---|---|---|
| Length | Any length, often 2–12 months | Under 28 consecutive days |
| Who offers it | A tenant who's leaving temporarily and plans to return | A host renting their principal residence |
| Permission needed | Landlord's consent (which can't be unreasonably refused) | City registration |
| Who you pay | The original tenant, who keeps paying the landlord | The host, usually through a platform |
| Typical booking | Direct agreement | Platform listing with an STR number |

If you're subletting, ask to see the tenant's lease and written proof the landlord consented. A tenant who's leaving permanently is doing an **assignment**, not a sublet, and you'd take over their lease. Our guide to [sublets and assignments in Ontario](/blog/sublet-and-assignment-ontario/) walks through both.

One more thing for renters thinking of hosting: the City doesn't require a tenant to get landlord consent to register a short-term rental, but recommends confirming that your lease allows it or getting written consent, because your landlord can still take tenancy issues to the LTB. Condo rules may ban short-term rentals outright. And tell your insurer first; renting your home out without disclosing it can void your coverage. See [tenant insurance in Ontario](/blog/tenant-insurance-ontario/).

## How to avoid short-term rental scams

Fake furnished listings target people who can't view in person. Watch for these signs:

- **No STR registration number**, or one that doesn't match the address. The City publishes active registration numbers on its Open Data portal.
- **Payment outside the platform**: requests for e-transfer, wire or crypto, or for a deposit before any agreement exists.
- **Price far below** similar listings in the same area.
- **A host who can't meet or show the unit**, often claiming to be abroad.
- **Photos that appear elsewhere**, including on other short-term listings. A reverse image search takes a minute.
- **Pressure to decide now** because "others are interested".
- **Links to sites asking for banking or personal details.**

Safer habits:

- Book and pay through the platform, and keep all messages there.
- For longer stays booked directly, view in person or by live video with the person who'll sign the lease, and verify their identity.
- Never pay before you've seen the place (or a live video of it) and have a written agreement.
- If you're scammed, report it to the Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre and Toronto Police, and to the platform.

Our guide to [Toronto rental scams](/blog/toronto-rental-scams/) has a longer checklist, and the [rental viewing checklist](/blog/rental-viewing-checklist-toronto/) helps once you're standing in the unit.

## Bottom line

For stays under 28 nights, book only registered short-term rentals in a host's principal residence and pay through the platform. For longer furnished stays, find out whether you're getting an RTA tenancy, ask for the standard lease, and treat sublets as agreements that need the landlord's consent.

## FAQ

**What counts as a short-term rental in Toronto?**
Under the City of Toronto's rules, a short-term rental is all or part of a home rented for less than 28 consecutive days in exchange for payment. It includes bed and breakfasts but not hotels, motels or student residences run by publicly funded or non-profit schools. Stays of 28 consecutive days or more aren't short-term rentals under the bylaw.

**How do I know a Toronto short-term rental is legal?**
Check that the listing shows a City-issued registration number in the format STR-0000-XXXXXX. Short-term rentals are only allowed in the operator's principal residence, and the City advises against booking any listing without a registration number. You can report unregistered or unsafe short-term rentals to 311.

**Does the Residential Tenancies Act apply to a furnished monthly rental?**
It depends on the arrangement, not the furniture. The Act generally doesn't apply to accommodation used on a seasonal or temporary basis, such as hotels, cottages or vacation rentals, or where you share a kitchen or bathroom with the owner. If you're renting a place as your home for months, ask the LTB or a legal clinic whether you're covered.

**Is a sublet the same as a short-term rental?**
No. A sublet is when a tenant moves out for a period, plans to return, and lets someone else live there with the landlord's consent. A short-term rental is a stay of under 28 consecutive days, often booked through a platform, that must be registered with the City and be the operator's principal residence.

**How can I avoid short-term rental scams in Toronto?**
Book and pay through the platform rather than by e-transfer or wire to a host, check for a valid STR registration number, reverse-search the photos, and be wary of prices far below similar listings or hosts who push you to move the conversation elsewhere. Report fraud to the Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre and local police.
