# Tenant Insurance Ontario: What It Covers and Who Needs It

URL: https://www.colivease.ca/blog/tenant-insurance-ontario/
Language: English
Updated: 2026-11-03

Tenant insurance in Ontario explained: contents, liability and living expenses, common exclusions, when a lease can require it, roommates and how to choose.

Tenant insurance (also called renters insurance) is a home insurance policy for people who rent. In Ontario it typically covers three things: your **belongings**, your **personal liability** if you accidentally injure someone or damage someone else's property, and **additional living expenses** if your place becomes unliveable after an insured loss. It isn't required by law, but your lease can require liability coverage.

Here's what's usually covered, what isn't, how it works with roommates and how to pick a policy.

## Key takeaways

- **Your landlord's insurance doesn't cover your things.** It's written for the landlord's building and liability.
- **Three core parts:** contents, liability and additional living expenses (ALE).
- **A lease can require liability insurance.** Section 11 of the standard lease covers this, and you must show proof if asked.
- **Roommates usually need separate policies.** Unrelated roommates aren't normally covered under yours.
- **Read the exclusions.** Flood, sewer backup and high-value items often need add-ons or have limits.

*This is general information, not legal or insurance advice. For your situation, talk to a licensed insurance agent or broker, and for tenancy questions contact the [Landlord and Tenant Board](https://tribunalsontario.ca/ltb/) or a community legal clinic through Legal Aid Ontario or Steps to Justice.*

## What tenant insurance covers

### 1. Your belongings (contents)

Clothes, furniture, electronics, kitchen gear and most household items, both in your unit and, under many policies, while you're away from home. You'll usually choose between two styles of coverage:

- **All risks (comprehensive):** covers loss from any cause except those the policy specifically excludes.
- **Named perils:** covers only the causes listed, such as fire, theft, smoke, vandalism or sudden water damage from plumbing or appliances.

All-risks coverage is broader and usually costs more.

### 2. Personal liability

If you're found legally responsible for injuring someone or damaging their property, liability coverage pays, up to your chosen limit, what you'd owe plus the cost of defending you in a lawsuit. For renters, a common example is a kitchen fire or overflowing bathtub that damages the unit below or the building itself. You can often raise your liability limit.

### 3. Additional living expenses (ALE)

If a fire or other insured loss makes your home unliveable, ALE pays the **extra** cost of living elsewhere, such as a hotel or temporary rental and higher food or laundry costs. It doesn't pay all your expenses, only the increase, and it's subject to limits. Keep every receipt.

## What it usually doesn't cover

| Gap | What to know |
|---|---|
| Flood and sewer backup | Overland flooding and sewer or drain backup are often optional add-ons. Ask, especially for basement units. |
| Wear, tear and maintenance | Insurance isn't a maintenance plan. Gradual deterioration isn't covered. |
| Your own injuries | The liability section covers harm to others, not to you or members of your household. |
| High-value items | Jewellery, fine art and collections are subject to specific limits. You may need to list them separately. |
| Unrelated roommates | Your policy covers you and certain family members, not housemates. |
| Business use or renting out | Tell your insurer before running a home business or renting your place short- or long-term. Not disclosing it can void coverage. |

The building itself, and appliances the landlord owns, are the landlord's to insure. Your policy covers your property and your liability.

## Can a landlord require tenant insurance in Ontario?

**Yes, if it's in the lease.** Section 11 of Ontario's standard lease lets the landlord and tenant agree whether the tenant must have **liability insurance**. If you agreed to it and the landlord asks for proof, you must provide it. Contents insurance for your own belongings is up to you.

A few practical points:

- Check section 11 of the lease **before** signing. If it's ticked, budget for a policy from move-in day.
- Ask what liability limit the landlord wants and get it in writing.
- Changes to a lease after it's signed must be agreed to in writing by both of you. Our [guide to Ontario's standard lease](/blog/ontario-standard-lease/) walks through each section.
- Insurance isn't a deposit. A landlord in Ontario can't ask for a damage deposit instead of, or on top of, insurance. See [rent deposit rules in Ontario](/blog/rent-deposit-rules-ontario/).

## Tenant insurance with roommates

Shared homes create shared risks, but insurance is usually individual.

- **Each roommate buys their own policy.** Home and tenant policies typically cover the policyholder, a spouse or partner, children and relatives living in the household. An unrelated roommate isn't on your policy, and their laptop isn't covered by yours.
- **Liability still matters for shared spaces.** If a roommate's candle starts a fire in the living room, the damage to the building and to other units can be large. Everyone carrying liability coverage protects the whole household.
- **Agree on minimums.** Put "each of us keeps tenant insurance with at least $X in liability" in your [roommate agreement](/blog/roommate-agreement-ontario/), and share proof once a year.
- **Students:** some home policies extend coverage to dependants under 21 who are students temporarily living away from home. Ask your parents' insurer before buying a separate policy, and confirm whether liability applies at your Toronto address.

If you're forming a household from scratch, it's a good topic to raise early. When you [ask a potential roommate questions](/blog/questions-to-ask-a-roommate/), add "Do you have tenant insurance?" to the list.

## How to choose a policy

### 1. Make a home inventory

Walk through each room and list what you own, with rough replacement values. Take photos or a video and keep receipts for expensive items. This tells you how much contents coverage you need and makes a future claim much easier.

### 2. Decide on the key choices

- **Contents amount:** enough to replace everything you own.
- **All risks or named perils.**
- **How claims are paid:** ask whether belongings are paid at replacement cost or at a depreciated value.
- **Liability limit:** at least what your lease requires.
- **Deductible:** a higher deductible lowers the premium but means you pay more per claim.
- **Add-ons:** sewer backup, overland water, and scheduled items like jewellery or a bike.

### 3. Understand what affects the price

We're not quoting prices here because they vary widely by insurer and situation. The factors insurers commonly weigh include:

- the value of your contents and the coverage type you choose
- where you live, since insurers track claims by neighbourhood
- the building, including its age, wiring, plumbing, heating and whether there are smoke and CO alarms
- your personal claims history
- your deductible and any add-ons
- any discounts the insurer offers

### 4. Buy from a licensed provider

In Ontario, insurance providers must be licensed. **Brokers** compare policies from several insurers; **agents** represent a single company. You can check a broker's licence on the Registered Insurance Brokers of Ontario (RIBO) directory.

Before you sign, ask:

- What exactly is excluded?
- Are my belongings covered when I'm away from home?
- What are the limits on electronics, bikes and jewellery?
- Does ALE have a dollar or time limit?
- Do I need to tell you if I sublet, take in a roommate or work from home?

## If you need to make a claim

1. **Report it quickly** to your insurer, with complete and accurate details. For theft, also report to police.
2. **Document everything:** photos of damage, a list of damaged or stolen items, receipts and any police report.
3. **Keep damaged items** unless they're unsafe, and check with your insurer before throwing anything out.
4. **Ask about ALE** if you can't stay in your home.
5. **Complete the proof of loss form.** It's typically due within 30 days.

If you disagree with a decision, use your insurer's internal complaints process first. If that doesn't resolve it, the General Insurance OmbudService (GIO) offers independent dispute resolution for its member insurers.

## Bottom line

Tenant insurance protects the things your landlord's policy doesn't: your belongings, your liability and your costs if you're displaced. Check whether your lease requires liability coverage, have each roommate get their own policy and choose coverage based on a real inventory, not a guess.

## FAQ

**Is tenant insurance mandatory in Ontario?**
No law requires every tenant to buy it. But Ontario's standard lease lets a landlord and tenant agree that the tenant must carry liability insurance, and if you agreed, you must show proof when the landlord asks. Contents insurance for your own belongings is always your choice, though it's strongly worth considering.

**Does my landlord's insurance cover my belongings?**
No. A landlord's policy is written for the landlord. It covers their building and their own liability, not your furniture, laptop or clothes. If there's a fire, flood or break-in, your things are only covered if you have your own tenant policy, or in some cases a parent's policy if you're a student dependant.

**Can roommates share one tenant insurance policy?**
Usually not. A home or tenant policy generally covers you, your spouse or partner, your children and relatives who live with you, not unrelated roommates. Most roommates each buy a separate policy for their own belongings and liability. If you want a combined policy, ask the insurer directly and get the answer in writing.

**What does tenant insurance not cover?**
Common gaps include flood and sewer backup unless you add them, damage from wear and tear or poor maintenance, injuries to you or people in your own household under the liability section, and high-value items like jewellery above set limits. Running a business or renting your place to others can also affect coverage if you don't tell your insurer.

**Am I covered under my parents' home insurance as a student?**
Possibly. Many home policies extend some coverage to dependants under 21 who are students temporarily living away from home. Limits and conditions vary, so ask your parents' insurer what's covered at your Toronto address and whether liability applies there, before you decide you don't need your own policy.

## Sources

- [Types of Home Coverage (Insurance Bureau of Canada)](https://www.ibc.ca/insurance-basics/home/types-of-home-insurance-coverage)
- [How Home Insurance Rates Are Set (Insurance Bureau of Canada)](https://www.ibc.ca/insurance-basics/home/how-home-insurance-rates-are-set)
- [How to Buy Home Insurance (Insurance Bureau of Canada)](https://www.ibc.ca/insurance-basics/home/how-to-buy-home-insurance)
- [How to File a Home Insurance Claim (Insurance Bureau of Canada)](https://www.ibc.ca/insurance-basics/home/how-to-file-a-home-insurance-claim)
- [Guide to Ontario's standard lease (Government of Ontario)](https://www.ontario.ca/page/guide-ontarios-standard-lease)
- [Property and Other Insurance (Financial Services Regulatory Authority of Ontario)](https://www.fsrao.ca/consumers/property-and-other-insurance)
- [Broker Search (Registered Insurance Brokers of Ontario)](https://www.ribo.com/consumer-information/licensee-directory-status/broker-search/)
- [Dispute Resolution (Insurance Bureau of Canada)](https://www.ibc.ca/insurance-basics/how-insurance-works/dispute-resolution)

# TTC Commute Guide: Choosing Where to Rent in Toronto

URL: https://www.colivease.ca/blog/ttc-commute-guide-renters/
Language: English
Updated: 2026-11-03

Choose where to rent in Toronto by commute: TTC subway lines, streetcars, Line 5 and Line 6 LRTs, 2026 fares, monthly fare capping and testing a commute first.

To choose where to rent in Toronto by commute, start from where you need to be, then look for homes within a short walk of a frequent rapid transit line (subway Lines 1, 2 or 4, or the new Line 5 Eglinton and Line 6 Finch West LRTs) that gets you there with one transfer or fewer. Before you sign, test the trip at rush hour. With PRESTO or a tapped bank card, an adult TTC fare is $3.30 and includes a two-hour transfer, and since September 2026 your trips are free after 47 paid trips in a month.

Here's how the network fits together, what it costs in late 2026, and how to estimate a commute properly.

## Key takeaways

- **Rapid transit first.** Living within a 10-minute walk of a subway or LRT station usually beats a closer address that relies on one slow bus.
- **Count transfers, not kilometres.** Each transfer adds waiting time and risk.
- **Fares (ttc.ca):** $3.30 adult with PRESTO, debit or credit; $3.35 cash.
- **Monthly fare capping:** free TTC trips after 47 paid trips in a calendar month, if you tap the same way every time.
- **Line 5 Eglinton and Line 6 Finch West are open**, which changes the math for midtown and northwest Toronto.

## The rapid transit network in late 2026

| Line | Route | Good to know |
|---|---|---|
| Line 1 Yonge-University | U-shaped line from Finch and Vaughan Metropolitan Centre through Union Station | The backbone for downtown commutes |
| Line 2 Bloor-Danforth | East-west from Kipling to Kennedy | Connects with Line 1 at St George, Bloor-Yonge and Spadina |
| Line 4 Sheppard | Short line from Sheppard-Yonge to Don Mills | Useful along Sheppard Avenue East; transfer to Line 1 at Sheppard-Yonge |
| Line 5 Eglinton | LRT with 25 stations and stops from Mount Dennis to Kennedy | Connects with Lines 1 and 2 and two GO lines |
| Line 6 Finch West | 11 km LRT with 18 stations and stops from Finch West Station (Line 1) to Humber College Station | Serves Humber Polytechnic's North Campus |

### Line 5 Eglinton: open, in a phased start

Line 5 began a phased opening on **February 8, 2026**. The TTC said the introductory period would let it fine-tune operations before announcing full, regularly scheduled service, and that end-to-end trips would take about 50 to 55 minutes, compared with up to 105 minutes by bus. From **April 5, 2026**, train service was extended later into the night, with trains about every four minutes at the busiest times. Metrolinx describes the full line as up to 60% faster than before for crossing the city. Because service details were still being adjusted during 2026, check ttc.ca for current hours before relying on a late-night trip.

Line 5 makes midtown neighbourhoods along Eglinton, such as Mount Dennis, Forest Hill, Leaside and the Golden Mile area, far more practical for commuters heading downtown or across the city.

### Line 6 Finch West: open since December 2025

Line 6 opened on **December 7, 2025**. It runs from Finch West Station, where you can transfer to Line 1, to Humber College Station, with connections to about 30 TTC bus routes and to regional transit such as MiWay and York Region Transit. From March 15, 2026, the TTC extended train service to 1 a.m. daily.

### Line 3 Scarborough: replaced by buses

The old Line 3 Scarborough is closed. Replacement bus routes now use the Scarborough Busway, built along part of the former Line 3 corridor, between Kennedy Station and Ellesmere Road.

## Streetcars, buses and late-night service

- **Streetcars** cover much of downtown and the inner neighbourhoods. They're convenient but can be slow in traffic.
- **Buses** fill in the rest of the city and feed into subway and LRT stations.
- **Blue Night Network** routes run overnight on most major routes, from about 1:30 a.m. until subway service starts, every 30 minutes or better. If you work late shifts, check whether a 300-series Blue Night route serves the address.

On Line 5 and Line 6 there's **no onboard payment**: pay before boarding (tap, or use the cash machines on surface platforms) and keep your proof of payment.

## TTC fares in late 2026

According to ttc.ca:

| Payment | Adult | Youth (13-19) | Senior (65+) |
|---|---|---|---|
| PRESTO card | $3.30 | $2.35 | $2.25 |
| Debit or credit tap | $3.30 | $3.30 | $3.30 |
| Cash | $3.35 | $2.40 | $2.30 |

Children 12 and under ride free. Post-secondary students pay the adult fare per trip but can still buy a **Post-Secondary Student Monthly Pass ($128.15)**. A PRESTO card costs $4, or you can add PRESTO to your phone's wallet for free. Since March 2, 2026, PRESTO cards need enough balance to cover the full fare before you tap.

### Two-hour transfer

When you pay with a PRESTO card, PRESTO Ticket, or debit or credit card, a two-hour transfer applies automatically: further TTC taps within two hours of your first tap aren't charged again. Cash fares don't include the two-hour transfer.

**One Fare** means you pay only once when connecting between the TTC and GO Transit, Brampton Transit, Durham Region Transit, MiWay or York Region Transit, as long as you tap with PRESTO or a bank card (not cash or a PRESTO Ticket).

### Monthly fare capping

Monthly fare capping took effect on **September 1, 2026**, and most monthly passes were discontinued on August 31, 2026. How it works:

- Tap the **same** PRESTO card, debit or credit card, or phone every time.
- Once you've made **47 paid trips** in a calendar month, the rest of your TTC trips that month are free.
- A paid trip is the first tap that starts a two-hour transfer window; taps inside that window are free and don't count.
- Cash, PRESTO Tickets and paper transfers don't count toward the cap.
- Switching between a physical card and the same card in your phone counts as two separate payment methods.
- Keep tapping after you reach the cap, because your tap is your proof of payment.

At the adult PRESTO fare, 47 trips works out to $155.10 a month. A typical five-day commuter making two paid trips a day may not reach the cap every month, so they simply pay as they go. Post-secondary students who ride often may still save with the student monthly pass, which the TTC recommends they keep using.

## How to estimate a commute before you sign

1. **List your fixed destinations**: work or campus, plus anywhere you go two or more times a week.
2. **Plan with your real arrival time.** Use the TTC trip planner or a map app set to arrive at, say, 8:55 a.m. on a weekday.
3. **Add the hidden minutes:** the walk to the stop, the wait, each transfer and the walk at the other end.
4. **Do a test run** at rush hour before you sign. Notice crowding and whether you'd get a seat.
5. **Check the return trip late in the evening and on weekends**, when frequencies drop.
6. **Have a backup route** in case of a subway closure or a missed connection.
7. **Price it.** Two paid trips a day for most of the month is close to the cap, so budget around the capped amount if you commute daily and ride on weekends too.

### Quick rules of thumb

- One frequent line with no transfers beats a shorter distance with two transfers.
- A 15-minute walk to a subway station is often faster than a bus that comes every 15 minutes.
- The new Line 5 and Line 6 stations widen your options, so compare listings along those lines too, not just near Line 1 and Line 2.

For neighbourhood ideas, see [best Toronto neighbourhoods for students](/blog/best-toronto-neighbourhoods-for-students/) and [for young professionals](/blog/best-toronto-neighbourhoods-for-young-professionals/). Use our [rental viewing checklist](/blog/rental-viewing-checklist-toronto/) to plan the commute test around your viewing, and weigh transit costs against rent with our guide to the [cost of renting a room in Toronto](/blog/cost-of-renting-a-room-in-toronto/).

## Let commute shape your search

## Bottom line

Pick the line before you pick the apartment. Aim for a short walk to Line 1, 2, 4, 5 or 6 with one transfer or fewer, test the trip at rush hour, and budget using the 2026 fares: $3.30 per adult PRESTO trip with free TTC rides after 47 paid trips a month. Check ttc.ca for the latest service changes before you sign.

*This article is general information, not legal or financial advice, based on ttc.ca and Metrolinx pages checked in November 2026. Fares, service hours and policies change, so confirm details on ttc.ca. For questions about your lease or rights as a renter, contact the Landlord and Tenant Board or a community legal clinic.*

## FAQ

**How much is a TTC fare in 2026?**
According to ttc.ca, an adult fare is $3.30 with a PRESTO card or a tapped debit or credit card, and $3.35 in cash. PRESTO fares for youth (13 to 19) are $2.35 and for seniors $2.25, and children 12 and under ride free. Paying with PRESTO or a card also gives you a two-hour transfer; cash does not.

**How does TTC monthly fare capping work?**
Since September 1, 2026, if you tap the same PRESTO card, debit or credit card, or phone every time, your TTC trips are free after 47 paid trips in a calendar month. A paid trip is the first tap that starts a two-hour transfer window. Cash and PRESTO Tickets don't count, and the count resets on the first of each month.

**Is Line 5 Eglinton open?**
Yes. Line 5 Eglinton began a phased opening on February 8, 2026, with 25 stations and stops between Mount Dennis and Kennedy, connecting with Lines 1 and 2. The TTC extended its hours from April 5, 2026 as it worked toward full regular service. Check ttc.ca for current hours and any service changes.

**Can I still buy a TTC monthly pass?**
Most monthly passes were discontinued on August 31, 2026, when fare capping started. The Adult 12-Month Pass and the Post-Secondary Student Monthly Pass, which ttc.ca lists at $128.15, are still available. Other riders now rely on monthly fare capping instead of buying a pass upfront.

**How do I test a commute before signing a lease?**
Use the TTC trip planner or a map app with your real arrival time, then do the trip yourself at rush hour on a weekday. Note the walk to the stop, the wait, transfers and crowding. Check the route again for late evenings and weekends, and see whether a Blue Night route serves the area if you work late.

## Sources

- [Fares and passes (TTC)](https://www.ttc.ca/Fares-and-passes)
- [TTC monthly fare capping (TTC)](https://www.ttc.ca/riding-the-ttc/Updates/TTC-monthly-fare-capping)
- [TTC to begin phased start to service on Line 5 Eglinton (TTC, February 2026)](https://www.ttc.ca/news/2026/February/TTC-to-begin-phased-start-to-service-on-Line-5-Eglinton)
- [Line 5 Eglinton train service to run later (TTC, April 2026)](https://www.ttc.ca/news/2026/April/Line-5-Eglinton-train-service-to-run-later-starting-Sunday)
- [Now open: Line 6 Finch West (TTC)](https://www.ttc.ca/riding-the-ttc/Line-6-Finch-West)
- [Scarborough Busway (TTC)](https://www.ttc.ca/riding-the-ttc/Updates/Scarborough--Busway)
- [Eglinton Crosstown LRT (Metrolinx)](https://www.metrolinx.com/en/projects-and-programs/eglinton-crosstown-lrt)

# Utilities for Renters in Toronto: Who Pays What

URL: https://www.colivease.ca/blog/utilities-for-renters-toronto/
Language: English
Updated: 2026-11-03

Utilities for Toronto renters: hydro, gas, water and internet, how to read what your lease includes, setting up accounts, splitting bills and ways to save.

In Toronto, who pays utilities depends entirely on your lease: electricity ("hydro") usually comes from Toronto Hydro or a building's sub-meter company, natural gas from Enbridge Gas, water from the City of Toronto (billed to the property owner), and internet from whichever provider you choose. Check the "Services and utilities" section of your lease before you sign, then set up any accounts in your name before move-in day.

Here's what each utility is, how to tell what's included, and how to split and cut the bills.

## Key takeaways

- **Your lease decides.** Ontario's standard lease has a section on who pays for electricity, heat and water.
- **Hydro:** Toronto Hydro, or a unit sub-meter provider in many condos.
- **Gas:** Enbridge Gas, mostly relevant if your unit has its own gas heating or appliances.
- **Water:** billed by the City to the owner, so tenants usually reimburse the landlord if the lease says so.
- **Internet:** almost always your choice and your account, unless rent includes it.

## Who provides what in Toronto

| Utility | Provider | Who usually holds the account |
|---|---|---|
| Electricity | Toronto Hydro, or a unit sub-meter provider (USMP) in many condos and newer buildings | Tenant if the unit has its own meter and the lease says so; otherwise the landlord |
| Natural gas (heat, hot water, stove) | Enbridge Gas | Landlord in most apartment buildings; tenant in some houses and townhomes |
| Water, sewer, garbage | City of Toronto | Property owner |
| Internet, TV, mobile | Your choice of provider | Tenant, unless included in rent |
| Hot water tank rental | Varies | Check the lease; often the owner in houses |

## How to tell what your lease includes

Most Ontario tenancies signed since April 30, 2018 must use the government's standard lease. In it:

- **Section 5** shows the base rent plus any separate charges, such as parking.
- **Section 6 (Services and utilities)** says which services are included and who is responsible for electricity, heat and water.

For room rentals, especially where you live with the owner, there may be no standard lease. In that case, ask for a written list of what's included, for example: "Rent includes heat, hydro, water and Wi-Fi." Vague phrases like "utilities included" can lead to arguments later about air conditioning or a space heater.

Questions to ask before you sign:

1. Which utilities are in my name, and which are included?
2. Is the unit separately metered for electricity? By Toronto Hydro or a sub-meter company?
3. Is heating gas, electric baseboard or a heat pump? (Electric heat can make winter hydro bills much higher.)
4. Is there a hot water tank rental, and who pays it?
5. Can you share a recent bill or a rough monthly average?

Our [Ontario standard lease guide](/blog/ontario-standard-lease/) explains the rest of the form.

## Setting up your accounts

### Hydro (Toronto Hydro)

If you're responsible for electricity and your unit has its own Toronto Hydro meter, open an account through Toronto Hydro's **start, stop, move** page or by phone at 416-542-8000 (weekdays, 8 a.m. to 8 p.m.). Do it at least a week or two before move-in so the account starts on your move-in date.

In many condos, electricity, and sometimes water, is billed by a unit sub-meter provider rather than Toronto Hydro. Your landlord or the building's management office can tell you which company to call.

### Gas (Enbridge Gas)

If gas is in your name, submit your move online through Enbridge's move page. You'll need the address and your move-in date. Enbridge notes that a one-time **New Account Charge** appears on your first bill when you move to a new property.

### Water (City of Toronto)

The City bills water, sewer and solid waste charges to the property owner. An owner can ask the City to mail bills to a tenant as their designate, but the City says the owner remains responsible for full payment. If your lease says you reimburse water, ask to see each bill.

### Internet

Compare plans on speed, price after any promotional period, contract length, and installation or equipment fees. In a shared home, agree who holds the account, since that person is on the hook for the contract.

## Understanding electricity prices

The Ontario Energy Board (OEB) sets electricity prices for Regulated Price Plan customers once a year on November 1. Prices set for **November 1, 2026**:

| Plan | Period (winter, weekdays) | Price (¢/kWh) |
|---|---|---|
| Time-of-Use (TOU) | Off-peak: 7 p.m. to 7 a.m., plus weekends and holidays | 9.1 |
| | Mid-peak: 11 a.m. to 5 p.m. | 14.6 |
| | On-peak: 7 to 11 a.m. and 5 to 7 p.m. | 18.9 |
| Ultra-Low Overnight (ULO) | Every day 11 p.m. to 7 a.m. | 3.7 |
| | Weekend off-peak: 7 a.m. to 11 p.m. | 9.1 |
| | Mid-peak: 7 a.m. to 4 p.m. and 9 to 11 p.m. | 14.6 |
| | On-peak: 4 to 9 p.m. | 37.7 |
| Tiered | First 1,000 kWh a month (winter) | 11.2 |
| | Above that | 13.2 |

These are electricity prices only. Your bill also includes delivery and regulatory charges and the Ontario Electricity Rebate, so the total cost per kWh is higher. TOU hours flip in summer (May 1 to October 31), when midday becomes on-peak.

Beware of door-to-door energy contracts. The OEB says fewer than one in 10 Ontario customers buy electricity from a retailer, and contract prices aren't regulated by the OEB.

## Heat and air conditioning rules

City of Toronto bylaw requires landlords to keep rental units at a minimum of **21°C from October 1 to May 15**. If a landlord provides air conditioning, it must run from June 1 to September 30 to keep the unit at no more than 26°C. If heat is your landlord's responsibility and your unit is cold, tell them in writing, and call 311 if it isn't fixed.

Under the Residential Tenancies Act, it's an offence for a landlord to withhold or interfere with vital services, including heat, electricity, natural gas, fuel and hot or cold water. Air conditioning isn't a vital service. If your building has suite meters, it's also an offence for a landlord to start charging you for electricity, or stop supplying it, without your consent. The province's Rental Housing Enforcement Unit deals with these offences.

## How to split bills between roommates

Pick a method, write it into your [roommate agreement](/blog/roommate-agreement-ontario/), and stick to it.

- **Equal split.** Simplest and works for most homes.
- **Per-person split for variable bills.** Hydro and gas split by the number of people actually living there, which helps when a partner is staying over a lot (see our [guest rules guide](/blog/roommate-guest-rules/)).
- **Weighted split.** Someone with a much larger room, a home office running all day, or a private space heater pays a bigger share.

Practical rules:

- One person per account; spread the accounts around so no one carries all the risk.
- The account holder posts each bill in the group chat within a few days.
- Everyone pays their share within a set time, for example seven days.
- Settle final bills when someone moves out, including any final meter reading.

For splitting rent itself, see [how to split rent fairly](/blog/split-rent-fairly/).

## Ways to save

- **Choose the right price plan.** Toronto Hydro customers on the Regulated Price Plan can choose TOU, ULO or Tiered. ULO only pays off if you can shift a lot of use to overnight and avoid the 4 to 9 p.m. weekday on-peak.
- **Shift big loads** like laundry and the dishwasher to off-peak hours, without breaking your house's quiet hours.
- **Seal drafts** around windows and doors and ask your landlord about fixing gaps.
- **Watch space heaters.** Electric heaters running all day can drive up a winter bill quickly.
- **Check assistance programs.** The OEB's Ontario Electricity Support Program gives eligible lower-income households an ongoing monthly credit on their electricity bill, including some people billed by sub-meter companies. The OEB also lists emergency help for households behind on bills.
- **Bundle smartly.** For internet, check the price after the promo ends, not just the first-year rate.

When you're comparing places, a rental with utilities included can be worth more than it looks. Our guide to the [cost of renting a room in Toronto](/blog/cost-of-renting-a-room-in-toronto/) shows how to compare total monthly costs.

## Find a place where the costs are clear

## Bottom line

Read section 6 of your lease, confirm which accounts are yours, and set them up before move-in. Hydro comes from Toronto Hydro or a sub-meter company, gas from Enbridge, water from the City through the owner, and internet from whoever you choose. Split bills by a written rule, and pick the electricity plan that matches how your household actually uses power.

*This article is general information, not legal advice. For your specific situation, contact the Landlord and Tenant Board or a community legal clinic.*

## FAQ

**Who pays utilities in a Toronto rental?**
Whoever the lease says. Ontario's standard lease has a section where the landlord and tenant agree who is responsible for electricity, heat and water. Room rentals in shared houses often include everything, while condo and apartment rentals frequently include some utilities but leave hydro or internet to the tenant. Get it in writing before you sign.

**How do I set up Toronto Hydro as a renter?**
If your lease makes you responsible for electricity and your unit has its own Toronto Hydro meter, you can set up a new account online through Toronto Hydro's start, stop and move page, or call 416-542-8000. In many condos, electricity is billed by a unit sub-meter provider instead, so ask your landlord which company to contact.

**Can a tenant have the City of Toronto water bill in their name?**
The City bills water, sewer and solid waste charges to the property owner. An owner can ask the City to send bills to a tenant as their designate, but the owner remains responsible for full payment. If your lease says you pay water, agree with your landlord how you'll be shown the bill and reimburse them.

**What are Ontario's electricity prices in November 2026?**
For Regulated Price Plan customers, the Ontario Energy Board set new prices on November 1, 2026. Time-of-Use prices are 9.1, 14.6 and 18.9 cents per kWh for off-, mid- and on-peak. Ultra-Low Overnight is 3.7 cents from 11 p.m. to 7 a.m., but on-peak is 37.7 cents. Delivery and other charges are extra.

**How should roommates split utility bills?**
Most households split utilities equally, and put each account in one person's name with a clear deadline for paying them back. If someone uses a lot more, such as working from home with a space heater or having a frequent overnight guest, agree a different share in writing. A shared spreadsheet or bill-splitting app keeps everyone honest.

## Sources

- [Electricity rates, effective November 1, 2026 (Ontario Energy Board)](https://www.oeb.ca/consumer-information-and-protection/electricity-rates)
- [Ontario Electricity Support Program (Ontario Energy Board)](https://www.oeb.ca/consumer-information-and-protection/bill-assistance-programs/ontario-electricity-support-program)
- [Start, stop, move account (Toronto Hydro)](https://www.torontohydro.com/start-stop-move-account)
- [Move, change or close your service (Enbridge Gas)](https://myaccount.enbridgegas.com/my-account/Im-Moving)
- [Rental housing offences: vital services and suite meters (Government of Ontario)](https://www.ontario.ca/page/rental-housing-offences)
- [Adding a tenant/agent to receive utility bills (City of Toronto)](https://www.toronto.ca/services-payments/property-taxes-utilities/utility-bill/adding-a-tenantagent-to-receive-utility-bills/)
- [Indoor temperatures in apartment units (City of Toronto)](https://www.toronto.ca/community-people/housing-shelter/rental-housing-rights-information/housing-property-standards/indoor-temperatures-in-apartment-units/)
- [Guide to Ontario's standard lease (Government of Ontario)](https://www.ontario.ca/page/guide-ontarios-standard-lease)

# Best Toronto Neighbourhoods for Students (2026 Guide)

URL: https://www.colivease.ca/blog/best-toronto-neighbourhoods-for-students/
Language: English
Updated: 2026-11-03

The best neighbourhoods in Toronto for students, campus by campus: U of T, TMU, York, OCAD and the colleges, with TTC commutes, vibe and what to watch for.

The best neighbourhoods in Toronto for students are the ones with a direct, reliable transit link to your campus: the Annex, Harbord Village and Kensington-Chinatown for U of T St. George and OCAD; Church-Wellesley, Cabbagetown and St. Lawrence for TMU and George Brown; and the areas along Line 1, Line 6 or local bus routes near York, Humber, Seneca and the Scarborough campuses. If downtown rent stretches your budget, sharing a place a few subway stops further out usually saves more money than it costs in commute time.

## Key takeaways

- **Start from your campus, not the map.** A 25-minute ride with no transfers beats a "closer" place that needs two buses.
- **Downtown campuses** (U of T St. George, TMU, OCAD, George Brown) are walkable from several central neighbourhoods, but rooms there tend to cost the most.
- **Suburban campuses** (York, UTSC, UTM, Humber, Seneca, Centennial) are easier and usually cheaper to live near, but they lean heavily on buses and LRT lines.
- **Sharing is the norm.** U of T's own data puts the average room in Toronto at about $1,150 to $1,220 a month, well below a one-bedroom.
- **Check the basics** before signing: rooming-house licence, legal basement unit, and a real landlord you've verified.

## How to choose a student neighbourhood

Three filters do most of the work:

1. **Commute.** Look at the full door-to-door trip at the time your classes start, including walking and transfers. The TTC trip planner is more honest than "10 minutes to campus" in a listing.
2. **Budget.** Rent is only part of it. Utilities, internet and a transit pass can add a lot, so compare all-in costs. Our guide to the [cost of renting a room in Toronto](/blog/cost-of-renting-a-room-in-toronto/) breaks this down.
3. **Vibe.** Do you want late-night food and live music, or a quiet street where you can sleep before an 8 a.m. lab? Visit at night and on a weekend if you can.

## Neighbourhoods by campus at a glance

Travel times below are rough estimates for a typical weekday; check the TTC trip planner for your exact address.

| Campus | Neighbourhoods to look at | Main transit | Typical vibe | Watch out for |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| U of T St. George | Annex, Harbord Village, Kensington-Chinatown, Koreatown | Line 1, Line 2, walking | Lively, student-heavy | High demand in late summer |
| TMU | Church-Wellesley, Garden District, Cabbagetown, St. Lawrence | Line 1 (TMU and College stations) | Busy, central | Noise, small condo units |
| OCAD University | Grange Park, Queen West, Kensington, Chinatown | Line 1 (Osgoode, St Patrick), Queen streetcar | Artsy, walkable | Bar noise on Queen West |
| George Brown | St. Lawrence, Corktown, Distillery area; Annex for Casa Loma campus | King streetcar, Line 1 | Mix of condos and older homes | Construction, rising condo prices |
| York (Keele) | Area around campus, Downsview, along Line 1 north | Line 1 (York University, Pioneer Village), Line 6 transfer at Finch West | Suburban, student houses | Unlicensed rooming houses |
| UTSC and Centennial (Progress) | Highland Creek, Morningside, around Scarborough Centre | Buses; Line 2 ends at Kennedy | Quiet, residential | Bus-dependent commutes |
| UTM | Erin Mills and central Mississauga | MiWay buses, connection to Line 2 at Kipling | Suburban, car-friendly | Outside the TTC system |
| Humber (North) | Humber Summit, Rexdale, along Finch West | Line 6 Finch West to Humber College station | Suburban | Long trips to downtown |
| Seneca (Newnham) | Don Valley Village, Bayview Village, near Finch and Don Mills stations | Buses from Line 1 and Line 4 | Residential, diverse | Few options walking distance |

## Downtown campuses

### U of T St. George

The Annex is the classic choice: Victorian houses split into flats and rooms, bookstores, cafés along Bloor, and stations at Spadina, Bathurst and St. George. Harbord Village and the streets around Kensington Market and Chinatown are a short walk to most buildings. Koreatown and Christie Pits are a little further west on Line 2 and usually a touch cheaper.

If prices are too high, look along Line 2 to the west or along Line 1 north. The U of T Off-Campus Housing Finder, open to students with a UTORid, lists rooms and has a roommate search.

### Toronto Metropolitan University (TMU)

TMU sits at Yonge and Gould, right next to the renamed TMU station (formerly Dundas) and College station. Church-Wellesley Village and the Garden District are walkable, and Cabbagetown and St. Lawrence offer older streets with more character. The Danforth area along Line 2 is a solid alternative: ride to Bloor-Yonge and transfer south.

Expect noise and crowds around Yonge-Dundas. Many listings are small condo units, so check closet space and whether a "bedroom" actually has a window.

### OCAD University

OCAD's main building on McCaul Street is surrounded by Grange Park, Chinatown and Kensington Market, all walkable. Queen West is close and creative but loud on weekend nights. Osgoode and St Patrick stations on Line 1 make it easy to live further out on the subway.

### George Brown Polytechnic

George Brown (renamed from George Brown College in 2025) has several campuses, so check which one you'll attend most. For St. James near King and Jarvis, St. Lawrence and Corktown are walkable. The Waterfront campus is near Queens Quay East, a walk or short streetcar ride from Union Station. For the Casa Loma campus, the Annex and Seaton Village work well, with Dupont station on Line 1 nearby.

## Suburban campuses

### York University (Keele campus)

York University and Pioneer Village stations on Line 1 put the campus on the subway, so anywhere along the Spadina side of Line 1 is fair game, including Downsview and areas around Sheppard West. Line 6 Finch West, which opened in December 2025, connects to Line 1 at Finch West station and serves the corridor to the west.

Many houses right around campus rent rooms individually to students. That can be affordable and social, but check that a house with many separately rented rooms is properly licensed.

### U of T Scarborough and Centennial (Progress campus)

Line 3 Scarborough closed permanently in 2023 and was replaced by buses, so Line 2 now ends at Kennedy station. Both campuses are reached by bus. Living close by in Highland Creek, Morningside or around Scarborough Centre usually means a much shorter, more predictable commute than coming from downtown. These are quieter, residential areas with good food options, especially Asian restaurants and plazas.

### U of T Mississauga

UTM is in Mississauga, outside the TTC system, and served by MiWay buses, with connections to Line 2 at Kipling station. Most students live in Erin Mills or central Mississauga. If you'll be in Toronto often for work or friends, factor in the extra fare and travel time.

### Humber Polytechnic and Seneca Polytechnic

For Humber's North campus, Line 6 Finch West now runs to Humber College station, which makes living along Finch West or near Finch West station (Line 1) far more practical than before. Humber's Lakeshore campus is in south Etobicoke near Mimico and Long Branch, served by the Queen streetcar and the Lakeshore West GO line.

Seneca's Newnham campus is near Finch Avenue East and Highway 404. Students often live around Don Mills station (Line 4) or Finch station (Line 1) and take a bus. Seneca also has a campus on York's Keele campus, so check your timetable first.

## What to watch out for anywhere in the city

- **Basement units.** Many affordable rooms are in basements. Look for proper windows, a second exit and working smoke and carbon monoxide alarms.
- **Rooming houses.** Since March 31, 2024, multi-tenant houses in Toronto need a City licence, and operators must post it at the entrance.
- **Scams.** Rental scams spike before each term. Never send money before you've verified the landlord and seen the unit in person or on a live video call. Read our guide to [Toronto rental scams](/blog/toronto-rental-scams/).
- **Transit gaps.** A place near "a bus" is not the same as a place near frequent service. Check how often your route runs in the evening and on weekends.
- **Late-summer rush.** Demand peaks before September. If you're coming from abroad, see our [international student renting checklist](/blog/international-student-renting-toronto/).

## Finding roommates who fit

## FAQ

**Where do most U of T St. George students live off campus?**
Many live within walking distance in the Annex, Harbord Village and Kensington-Chinatown, or a short subway ride away along Line 1 and Line 2. Students on a tighter budget often share a house or apartment further out, such as along Line 2 west or in North York, and accept a longer ride.

**Is it better to live downtown or in North York as a student?**
Downtown wins on walkability and short commutes if your campus is downtown, but rooms usually cost more. North York along Line 1 tends to offer more space for the money and a direct subway ride, so it suits students at York, Seneca or anyone willing to commute about half an hour each way.

**What is the cheapest area in Toronto for students?**
There is no single cheapest area, and prices change street by street. In general, rooms in shared homes further from downtown, but still near a subway or LRT stop, cost less than downtown units. Compare the full cost including transit time before deciding.

**Is Scarborough a good place to live for U of T Scarborough or Centennial students?**
Yes, living near campus in Scarborough usually means a much shorter commute, since both campuses rely on buses rather than the subway. Areas like Highland Creek, Morningside and around Scarborough Centre are popular with students. Check bus frequency to campus before you sign.

**How do I check if a student rooming house is legal in Toronto?**
Since March 31, 2024, operators of multi-tenant (rooming) houses in Toronto need a City licence, and they must post the licence at the entrance. Ask to see it, and be cautious if a landlord renting many rooms separately cannot show one.

# 多伦多留学生住哪里？按学校选社区（2026）

URL: https://www.colivease.ca/zh/blog/best-toronto-neighbourhoods-for-students/
Language: Chinese (Simplified)
Updated: 2026-11-03

多伦多留学生住哪里最合适？按多大、TMU、约克、OCAD 和 Humber、Seneca 等学院逐一分析周边社区、TTC 通勤、生活氛围和避坑要点，选房前先看这篇。

多伦多留学生住哪里？一句话：**先看学校，再看地铁线**。在多伦多大学 (U of T) St. George 校区和 OCAD 读书，Annex、唐人街、Kensington 一带步行就能上课；在 TMU 和 George Brown 读书，可以看 Church-Wellesley、Cabbagetown、St. Lawrence；约克、Humber、Seneca 和士嘉堡几个校区，则要沿 1 号线、6 号线或公交线路找。市中心太贵的话，往外多坐几站地铁再找人合租，省下的钱通常比多花的通勤时间更值。

## 先说结论：几条核心建议

- **以通勤为第一标准**：不用换乘、单程 25 分钟左右的地方，往往比地图上更近、却要倒两趟公交的地方更省心。
- **市中心校区**（多大 St. George、TMU、OCAD、George Brown）周边步行可达的社区不少，但房租也最高。
- **郊区校区**（约克、UTSC、UTM、Humber、Seneca、Centennial）附近租房相对便宜，但通勤更依赖公交和轻轨。
- **合租是常态**：根据多大官方汇总的数据，多伦多一个房间的平均月租大约在 1,150 到 1,220 加元之间，明显低于一室公寓。
- **签约前查三件事**：合租屋有没有执照、地下室是否合规、房东身份是否核实过。

## 选社区的三个标准

1. **通勤时间**：按你上课的时间段，在 TTC 官网或地图软件里查"门到门"的时间，包括步行和换乘。房源里写的"10 分钟到学校"不一定靠谱。
2. **总预算**：房租只是一部分，水电、网费、交通费加起来不少。具体可以看我们的 [多伦多租房多少钱](/zh/blog/cost-of-renting-a-room-in-toronto/)。
3. **生活氛围**：你喜欢夜宵和热闹，还是需要早睡赶早课？有条件的话，晚上和周末各去看一次。

## 各校区周边社区一览

下表的通勤时间只是工作日的粗略估计，具体请用 TTC 行程规划查询你的地址。

| 校区 | 推荐看的社区 | 主要交通 | 氛围 | 需要注意 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 多大 St. George | Annex、Harbord Village、唐人街/Kensington、Koreatown | 1 号线、2 号线、步行 | 热闹、学生多 | 八月前后竞争激烈 |
| TMU | Church-Wellesley、Garden District、Cabbagetown、St. Lawrence | 1 号线 TMU 站、College 站 | 繁华、市中心 | 噪音大、公寓面积小 |
| OCAD | Grange Park、Queen West、唐人街 | 1 号线 Osgoode、St Patrick 站，Queen 有轨电车 | 文艺、好逛 | 周末酒吧噪音 |
| George Brown | St. Lawrence、Corktown、Distillery 一带；Casa Loma 校区看 Annex | King 有轨电车、1 号线 | 公寓和老房混合 | 施工多、租金上涨 |
| 约克 (Keele) | 学校周边、Downsview、1 号线北段 | 1 号线 York University、Pioneer Village 站 | 郊区、学生屋多 | 无执照合租屋 |
| UTSC、Centennial (Progress) | Highland Creek、Morningside、Scarborough Centre 周边 | 公交车，2 号线终点 Kennedy | 安静、住宅区 | 依赖公交 |
| UTM | Erin Mills、密西沙加市中心 | MiWay 公交，在 Kipling 站接 2 号线 | 郊区、偏车行 | 不在 TTC 系统内 |
| Humber (North) | Humber Summit、Rexdale、Finch West 沿线 | 6 号线 Finch West 到 Humber College 站 | 郊区 | 去市中心较远 |
| Seneca (Newnham) | Don Valley Village、Bayview Village、Finch 和 Don Mills 站附近 | 1 号线、4 号线转公交 | 住宅区、华人多 | 步行可达的房源少 |

## 市中心校区

### 多伦多大学 St. George 校区

Annex 是多大学生的"经典选择"：老式维多利亚风格的独立屋被分成一个个单元和房间，Bloor 街上书店、咖啡馆一条街，Spadina、Bathurst、St. George 几个地铁站都在附近。Harbord Village、唐人街和 Kensington Market 一带走路就能到大部分教学楼，买菜吃饭也方便。往西一点的 Koreatown 和 Christie Pits 在 2 号线上，价格一般稍微友好一些。

如果市中心实在太贵，可以沿 2 号线往西，或者沿 1 号线往北找。持有 UTORid 的同学可以使用多大官方的 Off-Campus Housing Finder，上面有房源，也有只限多大学生使用的找室友功能。

### TMU（多伦多都会大学）

TMU 位于 Yonge 和 Gould 街口，旁边就是原来的 Dundas 站，2025 年 12 月起正式改名为 TMU 站，College 站也很近。Church-Wellesley 和 Garden District 步行可达，Cabbagetown 和 St. Lawrence 的街区更有生活气息。2 号线上的 Danforth 一带也不错：坐到 Bloor-Yonge 换 1 号线往南几站就到。

Yonge-Dundas 附近人多、噪音大，很多房源是小户型公寓，看房时注意储物空间，以及所谓的"卧室"到底有没有窗户。

### OCAD 大学

OCAD 主楼在 McCaul 街，周围就是 Grange Park、唐人街和 Kensington Market，生活非常方便。Queen West 很有艺术气息，但周末晚上比较吵。1 号线的 Osgoode 站和 St Patrick 站都在附近，住远一点沿地铁通勤也很容易。

### George Brown Polytechnic

George Brown 在 2025 年由 George Brown College 更名为 George Brown Polytechnic，有好几个校区，先确认你主要在哪个校区上课。King 和 Jarvis 附近的 St. James 校区，可以看 St. Lawrence 和 Corktown；湖滨的 Waterfront 校区离 Union 站不远；Casa Loma 校区则适合住 Annex 或 Seaton Village，附近有 1 号线 Dupont 站。

## 郊区校区

### 约克大学 (York University) Keele 校区

1 号线的 York University 站和 Pioneer Village 站直接通到校园，所以 1 号线 Spadina 一侧沿线都可以考虑，比如 Downsview、Sheppard West 一带。2025 年 12 月开通的 6 号线 Finch West 轻轨在 Finch West 站与 1 号线换乘，覆盖 Finch 大道西段。

学校周边有很多独立屋把房间一个个分租给学生，价格相对便宜，也容易交朋友。但要留意：分别出租很多房间的房子，需要有市政府的多租户住宅执照。

很多同学会在约克论坛、51.ca 或微信群里找约克附近的房间，这些渠道信息多、更新快，但也是假房源和"二房东"纠纷的高发地。一定要实地或视频看房、核实对方身份后再付款。

### 多大士嘉堡 (UTSC) 和 Centennial (Progress 校区)

3 号线士嘉堡线已在 2023 年永久停运，改由公交替代，所以现在 2 号线的东端终点是 Kennedy 站，两个校区都要靠公交到达。住在附近的 Highland Creek、Morningside 或 Scarborough Centre 周边，通勤会比从市中心过来短得多，也更稳定。这一带比较安静，中餐和亚洲超市选择很多，对刚来的同学很友好。

### 多大密西沙加 (UTM)

UTM 在密西沙加 (Mississauga)，不属于 TTC 系统，当地公交是 MiWay，可以在 Kipling 站接 2 号线。大部分同学住在 Erin Mills 或密西沙加市中心。如果你经常要去多伦多打工或见朋友，要把额外的车费和时间算进去。

### Humber 和 Seneca

去 Humber 的 North 校区，现在可以坐 6 号线 Finch West 直达 Humber College 站，所以住在 Finch West 沿线或 1 号线 Finch West 站附近比以前方便多了。Humber 的 Lakeshore 校区在 Etobicoke 南部，靠近 Mimico 和 Long Branch，有 Queen 有轨电车和 GO 火车 Lakeshore West 线。

Seneca 的 Newnham 校区在 Finch 东和 404 号公路附近，周边华人家庭多，中文生活资源丰富。同学们常住在 4 号线 Don Mills 站或 1 号线 Finch 站附近，再坐公交去学校。Seneca 在约克大学校园内也有校区，先看清课表再决定住哪。

## 预算大概要准备多少

多大学生生活办公室 (UofT Student Life) 在 2026 年春季汇总了几组数据：根据多伦多市政府的数据和多大校外租房平台上的房源，多伦多一个房间的平均月租大约是 1,150 到 1,220 加元；一室公寓的平均水平明显更高，St. George 校区周边尤其贵。需要注意的是，这些都是平均数，市中心靠近地铁、带独立卫生间或者带家具的房间，通常会比平均价贵；士嘉堡、北约克等地离学校近的合租房间，则可能便宜一些。

做预算时，不要只看房租这一个数字，建议把下面几项一起算进去：

- **房租本身**，以及是否包水电、网费；
- **交通费**：住得远一点房租便宜，但公交时间和车费也要算；
- **租客保险**：很多房东会要求，价格不高，但能保障你的个人物品；
- **一次性开销**：第一个月房租、最后一个月房租押金、搬家和买家具的费用。

如果预算比较紧，最实际的办法通常是和同学合租一套两室或三室的房子，人均下来往往比单独租一个房间更划算，还多了客厅和厨房的空间。

## 去哪里找房比较靠谱

**优先用学校官方渠道。** 多大的 Off-Campus Housing Finder、约克大学的校外住房平台、TMU 的 Off-Campus Housing Office 都面向本校学生，有的还提供租房咨询或房东纠纷调解。需要注意的是，学校一般不会替你实地检查每一套房子，也不担保房源信息完全准确，但遇到问题时至少有校内的老师可以咨询。

**中文渠道用得好也很方便。** 很多同学会在微信群、小红书、51.ca 或约克论坛上找房、找室友，优点是沟通方便、信息更新快、能找到口味相近的室友。但这些地方也是假房源、冒充房东、"一房多租"的高发地，尤其是开学前的七八月。几个基本原则：

- 对方不肯视频或见面、只催你先转定金的，直接放弃；
- 价格明显低于同区域平均水平的，先打个问号；
- 不要随便把护照、学签的照片发给没核实过的人；
- 付款前确认对方确实是房东或有权出租的人，并签好书面租约。

**留学生最好先落地再定长租。** 条件允许的话，先订两三周的短租或临时住处，到了多伦多实地看房、感受通勤后再签一年的租约，能避免很多坑。

## 不管住哪，都要注意这些

- **地下室**：很多便宜房间在地下室。看房时检查有没有正常大小的窗户、第二个出口，烟雾和一氧化碳报警器是否能用。
- **合租屋执照**：2024 年 3 月 31 日起，多伦多的多租户住宅需要执照，经营者要在入口张贴执照。
- **诈骗**：每到开学季，小红书、微信群里的假房源就特别多。没有核实房东身份、没有实地或视频看房之前，千万不要转定金。详见 [多伦多租房防骗指南](/zh/blog/toronto-rental-scams/)。
- **公交班次**：离"某条公交线"近，不等于班次多。查一下晚上和周末的发车频率。
- **开学季抢房**：九月前需求最大，人在国内的同学可以先看 [多伦多留学生租房清单](/zh/blog/international-student-renting-toronto/)。

## 找到合得来的室友

## 常见问题

**多大 St. George 校区的学生一般住在哪里？**
很多人住在步行可达的 Annex、Harbord Village、唐人街和 Kensington Market 一带，或者沿 1 号线、2 号线坐几站地铁。预算紧的同学常常在更远一些的地铁沿线合租，用稍长的通勤换更低的房租。

**留学生住市中心好还是住北约克好？**
如果学校在市中心，住市中心通勤短、生活方便，但房租普遍更高。北约克 (North York) 沿 1 号线一带同样的预算往往能住得更宽敞，地铁直达，适合约克大学、Seneca 的学生，或者能接受单程半小时左右通勤的同学。

**多伦多哪个区租房最便宜？**
没有固定的最便宜社区，价格常常一条街一个样。总体来说，离市中心较远、但靠近地铁或轻轨站的合租房间比市中心的便宜。比较时要把通勤时间和交通费一起算进去。

**在士嘉堡 (Scarborough) 读书住哪里方便？**
多大士嘉堡校区 (UTSC) 和 Centennial 的 Progress 校区都主要靠公交车，住在学校附近的 Highland Creek、Morningside 或 Scarborough Centre 周边，通勤会短很多也更稳定。签约前先查好去学校的公交班次。

**怎么判断学生合租屋 (rooming house) 是否合法？**
自 2024 年 3 月 31 日起，多伦多的多租户住宅 (multi-tenant house) 经营者必须取得市政府执照，并在入口处张贴执照信息。看房时可以直接要求查看；如果房东分别出租很多个房间却拿不出执照，要多加小心。

## 参考资料

- [UofT Student Life：Rental costs in Toronto/GTA（多大租金数据）](https://www.studentlife.utoronto.ca/task/rental-costs-in-toronto-gta/)
- [UofT Student Life：Off-Campus Housing Finder（多大校外租房平台）](https://www.studentlife.utoronto.ca/service/off-campus-housing-finder/)

- [TTC：Dundas 站更名为 TMU 站、Eglinton West 站更名为 Cedarvale 站](https://www.ttc.ca/news/2025/December/Dundas-and-Eglinton-West-Stations-to-be-officially-renamed-as-of-December-7)
- [TTC：3 号线士嘉堡线停运后的替代公交](https://www.ttc.ca/news/2023/August/TTC-improving-Line-3-Scarborough-bus-shuttle-routes)

# Best Neighbourhoods to Rent in Toronto for Professionals

URL: https://www.colivease.ca/blog/best-toronto-neighbourhoods-for-young-professionals/
Language: English
Updated: 2026-11-03

The best neighbourhoods to rent in Toronto for young professionals: King West, Liberty Village, Yonge & Eglinton, North York and more, compared.

The best neighbourhoods to rent in Toronto as a young professional are the ones that match your commute and lifestyle: King West and the downtown core if you want to walk to the office and go out often, Liberty Village for a condo community with a short trip downtown, Yonge & Eglinton or North York Centre for a direct subway ride and more space for the money, and Leslieville, the Annex or the Danforth for a real neighbourhood feel. Each one trades off price, space, noise and commute differently, so decide which trade-off you can live with first.

## Key takeaways

- **Commute shapes everything.** A direct subway ride is usually more predictable than a streetcar, and a walk is better than both.
- **Downtown and King West** offer the shortest commutes and best nightlife, at the highest rents and smallest units.
- **Midtown and North York** along Line 1 give you more space for the money and a straight shot to the Financial District.
- **East and west-end neighbourhoods** like Leslieville, the Danforth and the Annex feel more residential but rely on streetcars or a transfer.
- **Newer condos aren't rent-controlled.** Units first occupied after November 15, 2018 are generally exempt from Ontario's rent increase guideline.

## How to compare neighbourhoods

Before you fall for a balcony view, run every option through four questions:

1. **What is the door-to-door commute at 8:30 a.m.?** Include walking, waiting and transfers. Streetcars share the road with traffic, so their travel times vary more than the subway's.
2. **How often will you actually go downtown?** If you're hybrid and in the office two or three days a week, a slightly longer commute in exchange for a second bedroom or home office can be a great deal.
3. **What does the all-in cost look like?** Condo rentals often bundle some utilities; house apartments may not. Ask what's included.
4. **What will you do on a Tuesday night?** Gym, park, groceries and a decent coffee within walking distance matter more over a year than a rooftop pool you use twice.

## Neighbourhood comparison

Commute times are rough weekday estimates to King and Bay; check the TTC trip planner for your exact address and start time.

| Neighbourhood | Getting to the Financial District | Main transit | Best for | Trade-off |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Downtown core / St. Lawrence | Walk, roughly 10–20 min | Line 1, King and Queen streetcars | Walking to work, events | Highest rents, small units |
| King West | Walk or streetcar, roughly 10–20 min | King streetcar | Restaurants, nightlife | Noise, weekend crowds |
| Liberty Village | Streetcar or GO, roughly 20–25 min | King streetcar, Exhibition GO | Condo community, gyms, dogs | Crowded streetcars, few routes in and out |
| The Annex | Subway, roughly 15 min | Line 1 and Line 2 | Character, cafés, culture | Older buildings, fewer amenities |
| Yonge & Eglinton | Subway, roughly 20 min | Line 1, Line 5 Eglinton | Midtown energy, new condos | Busy intersection, pricey |
| North York Centre | Subway, roughly 30 min | Line 1 | Space for the money, quieter | Longer commute, quieter nights |
| Leslieville | Streetcar, roughly 25 min | Queen and King streetcars | Brunch, parks, neighbourhood feel | Streetcar-dependent, construction |
| The Danforth | Subway with a transfer, roughly 20–25 min | Line 2 to Line 1 | Patios, houses split into flats | Transfer at Bloor-Yonge |

## The neighbourhoods up close

### Downtown core and St. Lawrence

If your office is near King and Bay, living downtown means walking to work, skipping transit delays and being close to everything from concerts to the waterfront. St. Lawrence, around the market, is a bit calmer than the towers near Union Station. Expect high rents for compact condo units and busy streets. This is a strong choice if you work long or unpredictable hours.

### King West

King West is restaurant-and-bar central, with converted warehouses and newer condos. The King streetcar runs along the street, but many people simply walk to the core. It's ideal if you're out several nights a week and don't mind noise on weekends. If you're a light sleeper, look at units facing away from King Street.

### Liberty Village

Liberty Village packs condos, gyms, grocery stores and coffee shops into a compact former industrial area. It's very popular with young professionals and dog owners. The catch is getting out: the King streetcar fills up at rush hour, and there are only a few streets in and out. Exhibition GO station on the Lakeshore West line is a handy alternative, one stop from Union.

### The Annex

The Annex mixes Victorian houses split into apartments, a few low-rise buildings and plenty of character. Bloor Street has bookstores, cafés and cinemas, and you're close to both Line 1 and Line 2. You'll trade modern amenities like in-suite laundry and gyms for charm, and you'll be living near the U of T crowd, which some love and some don't.

### Yonge & Eglinton

Midtown's busiest node has lots of newer condos, restaurants and shopping. Line 1 runs straight downtown, and Eglinton station is also an interchange with Line 5 Eglinton, which makes cross-town trips easier. It has a younger, professional feel and is generally a little cheaper than the core for similar space, though not cheap.

### North York Centre

Along Yonge between Sheppard and Finch, North York Centre offers taller buildings, larger units for the money and a straight Line 1 ride downtown. Line 4 Sheppard connects at Sheppard-Yonge. You'll find a big mix of Korean, Chinese and Persian restaurants along Yonge, and quieter evenings than downtown. Great if you value space and calm, less great if your social life is mostly in the core.

### Leslieville

East of the Don River, Leslieville is known for brunch spots, independent shops, parks and a strong neighbourhood identity. You'll find a mix of house apartments and newer mid-rise condos. Commutes rely on the Queen and King streetcars, and major transit construction for the Ontario Line is underway in parts of the area, which can mean noise and detours for now.

### The Danforth

Greektown and the surrounding Danforth neighbourhoods have patios, grocers and many houses split into upper and lower flats. Line 2 runs right under Danforth Avenue; to reach the Financial District, you'll transfer to Line 1 at Bloor-Yonge. It feels residential while staying well connected.

### Also worth a look

Roncesvalles and High Park on the west side offer a park-heavy, village feel on Line 2 and the King and Queen streetcars. Davisville, just south of Yonge & Eglinton, is a little quieter than its neighbour with similar transit access.

## Rent control, renewals and budgeting

Before signing, ask when the unit was first occupied. Ontario's rent increase guideline for 2026 is 2.1%, but most units first occupied after November 15, 2018, which includes many newer condos, are exempt from it. That means your rent could rise more at renewal. Our guide to the [2026 rent increase guideline](/blog/ontario-rent-increase-guideline-2026/) explains the details.

For budgeting, CMHC's benchmark is that housing is affordable when it costs less than 30% of before-tax income. In Toronto that's hard to hit alone: TRREB's rental report for the second quarter of 2026 put the average one-bedroom condo apartment leased across the GTA at about $2,270 a month. For a full breakdown of what renting costs, see our guide to the [cost of renting a room in Toronto](/blog/cost-of-renting-a-room-in-toronto/).

## Sharing as a professional

Plenty of young professionals in Toronto share a two-bedroom condo or a house rather than paying for a one-bedroom alone. It can free up money for savings or travel, and it often gets you a better location than you could afford solo. The key is finding someone whose schedule and habits fit yours. Our guide to [finding a roommate in Toronto](/blog/find-a-roommate-in-toronto/) covers how to vet people and set expectations.

## FAQ

**What is the best area in Toronto for young professionals?**
It depends on your priorities. King West and the downtown core suit people who want to walk to work and go out often, Yonge & Eglinton and North York Centre suit people who want more space and a direct subway ride, and Leslieville or the Annex suit people who want a neighbourhood feel close to downtown.

**Is Liberty Village a good place to live?**
Liberty Village is popular with young professionals for its newer condos, restaurants, gyms and dog-friendly streets. The main drawbacks are crowded King streetcars at rush hour and limited ways in and out. Exhibition GO station on the Lakeshore West line is an alternative to the streetcar for getting downtown.

**Is it worth living in North York and commuting downtown?**
For many renters, yes. Line 1 runs directly from North York Centre and Sheppard-Yonge to the Financial District, typically in about half an hour, and you often get more space or a newer building for the money. It is less ideal if you go out downtown most evenings.

**How much of my income should go to rent in Toronto?**
CMHC considers housing affordable when it costs less than 30% of a household's before-tax income, and that is a useful starting point for a budget. In Toronto many renters spend more, which is why sharing a larger unit with a roommate is common among young professionals.

**Are newer condo rentals in Toronto covered by rent control?**
In Ontario, most units first occupied for residential purposes after November 15, 2018 are exempt from the annual rent increase guideline. Older units are generally covered. Ask when the unit was first occupied before you sign, because it affects how much your rent can rise each year.

## Sources

- [Government of Ontario: Residential rent increases (2026 guideline)](https://www.ontario.ca/page/residential-rent-increases)
- [Government of Ontario: Renting in Ontario, your rights](https://www.ontario.ca/page/renting-ontario-your-rights)
- [CMHC: National Housing Strategy glossary (affordability)](https://www.cmhc-schl.gc.ca/nhs/guidepage-strategy/glossary)
- [TTC: Dundas and Eglinton West stations renamed](https://www.ttc.ca/news/2025/December/Dundas-and-Eglinton-West-Stations-to-be-officially-renamed-as-of-December-7)
- [TRREB: Rental market report, Q2 2026](https://public.trreb.ca/wp-content/files/market-stats/rental-reports/rental_report_Q2-2026.pdf)
- [UofT Student Life: Rental costs in Toronto/GTA](https://www.studentlife.utoronto.ca/task/rental-costs-in-toronto-gta/)

# 多伦多上班族住哪里？热门租房社区对比

URL: https://www.colivease.ca/zh/blog/best-toronto-neighbourhoods-for-young-professionals/
Language: Chinese (Simplified)
Updated: 2026-11-03

多伦多上班族住哪里最划算？对比市中心、King West、Liberty Village、Yonge & Eglinton、北约克等社区的通勤、生活方式和租房取舍。

多伦多上班族住哪里？答案取决于你最看重什么：想走路上班、下班常出去玩，选**市中心或 King West**；喜欢新公寓社区、通勤又不想太远，看 **Liberty Village**；想地铁直达、同样预算住得更宽敞，选 **Yonge & Eglinton 或北约克中心 (North York Centre)**；想要有烟火气的街区生活，可以考虑 **Leslieville、Annex 或 Danforth**。每个社区在房租、面积、噪音和通勤之间的取舍都不一样，先想清楚自己最能接受哪一种。

## 先说结论

- **通勤决定一切**：地铁比有轨电车准时，走路上班又比地铁更省心。
- **市中心和 King West** 通勤最短、夜生活最丰富，但房租最高、户型最小。
- **Midtown 和北约克**沿 1 号线，同样的钱住得更大，坐地铁直达金融区。
- **东西两边的老社区**（Leslieville、Danforth、Annex）生活气息浓，但要靠有轨电车或换乘。
- **新公寓不受涨租上限保护**：2018 年 11 月 15 日之后首次入住的单位，一般不受安省涨租指导线限制。

## 选社区前先问自己四个问题

1. **早上八点半出门，门到门要多久？** 把步行、等车、换乘都算上。有轨电车和汽车一起走路面，时间波动比地铁大。
2. **一周真正去几天办公室？** 如果是混合办公、每周去两三天，通勤稍长一点、换来多一个房间做书房，往往很值。
3. **全部算下来每月花多少？** 公寓楼的房租常常包含部分水电，独立屋分租的单位不一定。签约前问清楚包含哪些费用。
4. **平时下班会做什么？** 健身房、公园、超市、好喝的咖啡在不在步行范围内，一年下来比一个只用过两次的天台泳池重要得多。

## 热门社区一览

下表通勤时间是工作日到 King 和 Bay 一带的粗略估计，具体请用 TTC 行程规划按你的地址和出门时间查询。

| 社区 | 到金融区 | 主要交通 | 适合谁 | 取舍 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 市中心 / St. Lawrence | 步行约 10–20 分钟 | 1 号线、King 和 Queen 有轨电车 | 想走路上班 | 房租最高、户型小 |
| King West | 步行或电车约 10–20 分钟 | King 有轨电车 | 爱美食和夜生活 | 噪音、周末人多 |
| Liberty Village | 电车或 GO 约 20–25 分钟 | King 有轨电车、Exhibition GO 站 | 喜欢公寓社区、养狗 | 电车挤、进出道路少 |
| Annex | 地铁约 15 分钟 | 1 号线、2 号线 | 喜欢老街区和文化氛围 | 老房子多、设施少 |
| Yonge & Eglinton | 地铁约 20 分钟 | 1 号线、5 号线 Eglinton | 喜欢 Midtown 的热闹 | 路口繁忙、租金不低 |
| 北约克中心 | 地铁约 30 分钟 | 1 号线 | 想要更大空间、更安静 | 通勤更长、晚上较冷清 |
| Leslieville | 电车约 25 分钟 | Queen 和 King 有轨电车 | 喜欢早午餐、公园 | 依赖电车、施工多 |
| Danforth | 地铁换乘约 20–25 分钟 | 2 号线转 1 号线 | 喜欢露台餐厅、老房 | 要在 Bloor-Yonge 换乘 |

## 逐个社区看

### 市中心和 St. Lawrence

如果你在 King 和 Bay 附近上班，住市中心就意味着走路上班，不怕地铁延误，看演出、去湖边都很方便。St. Lawrence 市场一带比 Union 站周边的高楼区安静一些。缺点很明显：小户型公寓也要高租金，街上总是人多。工作时间长、经常加班的人特别适合住这里。

### King West

King West 是餐厅和酒吧最集中的地方，有仓库改造的 loft，也有很多新公寓。King 有轨电车就在门口，但很多人干脆走路去金融区。适合一周出去玩好几晚、不介意周末吵闹的人。睡眠浅的话，挑不朝 King 街的单位。

### Liberty Village

这一片原来是工业区，现在公寓、健身房、超市、咖啡馆一应俱全，年轻上班族和养狗的人特别多。问题在于"出去难"：早高峰 King 有轨电车经常挤不上，进出的路也就几条。Exhibition GO 站在 Lakeshore West 线上，一站到 Union，是不错的替代方案。

### Annex

Annex 以维多利亚式老房分租的公寓为主，也有一些低层公寓楼，很有味道。Bloor 街上有书店、咖啡馆、电影院，1 号线和 2 号线都在附近。代价是很多房子没有室内洗衣机、健身房这些现代设施，而且周边多大学生多，有人喜欢这种氛围，也有人觉得吵。

### Yonge & Eglinton

这是 Midtown 最热闹的路口，新公寓、餐厅、商场集中。1 号线直通市中心，Eglinton 站现在还是 5 号线 Eglinton 的换乘站，东西向出行也方便了。整体氛围年轻、偏上班族，同样面积通常比市中心便宜一点，但也谈不上便宜。

### 北约克中心 (North York Centre)

Yonge 街 Sheppard 到 Finch 之间就是北约克中心，高楼多，同样的预算能租到更大的单位，坐 1 号线直达市中心，Sheppard-Yonge 站还能换 4 号线。Yonge 街上韩餐、中餐、波斯菜选择丰富，华人超市和中文服务也多，很多新移民落地第一站就选这里。晚上比市中心安静，适合重视空间和生活便利的人；如果社交主要在市中心，就要多考虑通勤。

### Leslieville

Leslieville 在 Don River 东边，以早午餐店、独立小店、公园和浓厚的社区感出名，有独立屋分租的单位，也有新建的中低层公寓。通勤主要靠 Queen 和 King 有轨电车。目前安省线 (Ontario Line) 在这一带部分路段施工，短期内会有噪音和绕行。

### Danforth

Greektown 和周边的 Danforth 社区有很多露台餐厅、蔬果店，以及上下层分租的独立屋。2 号线就在 Danforth 大道下面，去金融区要在 Bloor-Yonge 换 1 号线。住起来像住宅区，交通又不差。

### 其他值得看的

西边的 Roncesvalles 和 High Park 公园多，有小镇的感觉，有 2 号线和 King、Queen 有轨电车。Yonge & Eglinton 南边的 Davisville 交通条件类似，但更安静一些。

## 如果你不在市中心上班

上面的对比默认你在金融区上班，但很多新移民的工作地点并不在市中心。比如公司在北约克、Don Mills 一带，住北约克中心或 Sheppard 沿线就比住市中心更合理；如果在机场附近、密西沙加或万锦 (Markham) 上班，坐地铁进城再出城反而绕远，住在公司附近或者 GO 火车沿线可能更省时间。

另外，开车上班的人要把停车费算进去：市中心很多公寓的车位要另外收费，有的楼甚至一位难求；而北约克、士嘉堡的不少房子自带车位。总之，先确定你每天最常去的地方，再倒推住在哪里，比单纯看"哪个社区最火"更靠谱。如果你和伴侣或室友在不同地方上班，可以各自查一下通勤时间，选一个对双方都还能接受的中间点，比如地铁换乘站附近。

## 涨租、续约和预算

签约前一定要问：这个单位是哪一年首次入住的？安省 2026 年的涨租指导线是 2.1%，但大多数 2018 年 11 月 15 日之后首次入住的单位（包括很多新公寓）不受这个限制，续约时房租可能涨得更多。详细规则可以看 [安省 2026 年涨租指导线](/zh/blog/ontario-rent-increase-guideline-2026/)。

做预算时，可以参考 CMHC 的标准：住房支出低于税前收入的 30% 算可负担。在多伦多一个人住要做到并不容易：多伦多地区地产局 (TRREB) 2026 年第二季度的租赁报告显示，大多伦多地区通过 MLS 出租的一室公寓平均月租约 2,270 加元。完整的费用拆解可以看 [多伦多租房多少钱](/zh/blog/cost-of-renting-a-room-in-toronto/)。

## 新移民上班族租房的几点实用建议

**提前准备好申请材料。** 多伦多热门社区的好房子往往几天就租出去，房东通常会看申请表、身份证件、工作证明（在职信或 offer）、近期工资单或银行流水，以及以前房东的推荐信。刚落地、还没有加拿大信用记录的话，可以多准备一些收入和存款证明，具体做法见 [没有信用记录怎么租房](/zh/blog/renting-with-no-credit-history-canada/)。

**看清楚公寓楼的规定。** 很多公寓楼搬家要提前预约货梯，有的楼还对搬家时间、押金有自己的规定；有没有车位、储物间、访客停车，也要问清楚。这些细节不会写在房源标题里，但会实实在在影响你的生活。

**实地走一遍通勤路线。** 看房那天，最好按上班时间从房子出发走一趟：走到车站要多久、早高峰车上挤不挤、换乘方不方便。地图上看起来差不多的两个社区，实际体验可能差很多。

**留意周边施工。** 多伦多这几年地铁、轻轨和公寓楼都在大量施工，房子附近如果有大型工地，白天的噪音和绕路可能持续好几年。签约前在街上走一圈，或者问问楼里的住户。

## 上班族合租，越来越常见

很多年轻上班族选择和朋友或同事合租两室公寓或整栋独立屋，而不是一个人负担一室公寓。省下来的钱可以存起来或者旅行，也常常能住到一个人负担不起的好地段。关键是找到作息和习惯合得来的人。

找人时，很多华人会先在微信群、小红书或 51.ca 上看帖子，信息确实多，但冒充房东、一房多租的情况也不少。见面前先视频确认身份，签好租约前不要转钱。

## 常见问题

**多伦多上班族最推荐住哪个区？**
要看你更在意什么。想走路上班、下班常出去玩，选市中心或 King West；想要更大空间、地铁直达，选 Yonge & Eglinton 或北约克中心；想要有社区感又离市中心不远，可以看 Leslieville 或 Annex。

**Liberty Village 适合住吗？**
Liberty Village 新公寓多，健身房、超市、餐厅齐全，很受年轻上班族和养狗人士欢迎。主要缺点是早高峰 King 有轨电车很挤，进出的道路也少。可以考虑坐 GO 火车 Lakeshore West 线，从 Exhibition 站一站到 Union。

**住北约克去市中心上班划算吗？**
对很多人来说是划算的。从北约克中心或 Sheppard-Yonge 坐 1 号线可以直达金融区，单程一般半小时左右，同样的预算往往能租到更大或更新的房子。如果你几乎每晚都在市中心社交，就没那么合适了。

**房租占收入多少比较合适？**
加拿大按揭和住房公司 (CMHC) 的标准是，住房支出低于税前收入的 30% 算可负担，可以作为做预算的起点。在多伦多，不少租客实际花得更多，所以上班族合租两室公寓非常普遍。

**新公寓的房租受涨租上限保护吗？**
在安省，大多数 2018 年 11 月 15 日之后首次入住的单位，不受每年涨租指导线的限制，更早的单位一般受限。签约前问清楚单位首次入住的时间，这会影响你续租时房租能涨多少。

## 参考资料

- [安省政府：Residential rent increases（2026 年涨租指导线）](https://www.ontario.ca/page/residential-rent-increases)
- [安省政府：Renting in Ontario: Your rights](https://www.ontario.ca/page/renting-ontario-your-rights)
- [CMHC：National Housing Strategy 术语表（可负担住房定义）](https://www.cmhc-schl.gc.ca/nhs/guidepage-strategy/glossary)
- [TTC：Dundas 站和 Eglinton West 站更名公告](https://www.ttc.ca/news/2025/December/Dundas-and-Eglinton-West-Stations-to-be-officially-renamed-as-of-December-7)
- [TRREB：2026 年第二季度租赁市场报告](https://public.trreb.ca/wp-content/files/market-stats/rental-reports/rental_report_Q2-2026.pdf)
